Part Specs Have Changed - This is the part # for our 11 year old GE refrigerator but this auger's measurements are different than the part I was replacing. I had bought another, cheaper auger on Amazon that also had problems with measurements. Other users recommended grinding down the metal rod. I did not have a grinder so I returned that one. After installing this auger with all my original pieces it was binding some place. Couldn't see where. Auger would manually turn with extreme difficulty. I knew the motor could burn out if I reinstalled the housing it the way it was. I searched YouTube and checked the schematics for this part. My original auger had 2 metal washers plus a plastic spacer at the end closest to the plastic spirals. Different schematics showed either 2 plastic spacers or 1 plastic spacer; no metal washers I finally found a couple on YouTube that demonstrated the difference in measurements on their auger. They also had 2 metal washers. He was able to grind down the dent on the rod to allow all his original pieces to fit including the 2 metal washer. I was ready to return this auger as I did not have a grinder. I should not have to be a machinist to get a part to work. Taking a chance I put everything back on the rod in proper order except for the 2 metal washers. Everything works great. Ice cubes come out and cubes get crusher almost better than before. Have been using for about a week without any problems. Very happy except this took me much more time to figure out than required. Without this issue it would have taken less than 20 minutes for total install and a 5 star rating. Something in the specs for this auger has changed over the last 11 years.

Great quality, appearance and functionality. Installation was challenging. - Got this range hood to replace an over the range microwave/exhaust fan. It wasn’t something that would be visible after it was installed so I could live with it. It looks and works beautifully after I got it installed. I installed it myself which was mistake number one. Unless you are a serious do it your selfer, I recommend hiring someone to do the install and not just some handyman but an experienced appliance repairman. I added a photo of when the install was in process. I had to tap into the microwave electrical outlet box to run a wire out the wall for the hood as it is set up to be hard wired (no plug in cord included). I had to attach a couple of strips of wood under the cabinet to accept the screws to hang the hood on. I had to fight with the sheet metal ducting to get it to fit the hood properly. I screwed a couple of scrap boards into the unfinished side cabinets to support the hood while it was being jockeyed into place for the install and that made things a lot easier. There were trips to the hardware store for parts and even a special twelve inch extension for my drill in order to reach the support screws. There was also some sweating, a lot of cussing and some blood from minor lacerations. We are very happy with the end product. I loved the challenge and would do it again.

That seemed great, so I purchased it. I now see that these claims for this same filter are gone, and they recommend changing the filter at the regular time. (I'm just shaking my head...)

Finally, I don't know if it was a feature or using my filter for a year, but I had a horrible, terrible time getting their old filter out. The new filter went in fine; although the instructions didn't talk about running water through it, we ran about 10 quarts of water through it, and all has been well.

Kinda pricey understates it, no?
It's really a shortcut that, in the end, though stylish and handsome, is not necessary. Practice makes perfect. Items like this and steaming thermometers are aimed at new recruits in the coffee army who become frustrated during boot camp and finally want something that just works. Believe me, I understand, but immerse yourself in videos, online advice, and visit good coffee shops (no, not *$s!). Watch the baristas. Some shops offer classes. While it might seem silly to take a class in "milk chemistry" or such, it's not. You'll gain by watching, listening, and speaking with others trying to master the craft.

If you love the look of this pitcher, and I don't blame you if you do-- it's cool looking, for sure-- buy it. But if it's just that you're not having luck steaming milk with a new machine, keep working. Avoid gimmicks that promise you a no effort shortcut. In the end, you'll be a better barista if you just stick with it, get the advice and instruction you need, and finally (and you will) master producing creamy microfoam.

Cheers, mates.

Read everything - We are about a week into it and this machine works great so far. We have run about 3 gallons of water through it. However, there are a few things to note.

4) The "cleaning" mode doesn't seem to do a whole lot. The ad makes it look like it swirls, etc., but it just basically runs water through the system for a few minutes.

I can move a small amount of ice from the ramp into the bin and it will start again. Also, once the auto-shutoff is activated, it will allow about half of what is in it melt before it starts making ice automatically again unless you open and close the lid. This may be by design since they want you to remove all the ice to a freezer.
6) I thought there was a light in it but there is not. That's an aesthetic thing to me and probably wouldn't bother most people.

Also, when I originally purchased it, it said it wouldn't ship until November but it shipped in less than a week.

Do it right the first time and you won't have to fight with the dryer. - My 20 year old dryer decided that it was going to heat at it's hottest setting to the point of scalding my hands when removing the clothes from the dryer and causing a major case of wrinkles in my work Polo's. After going to YouTube to find out how to diagnose the issue, I found that there are a few things to check. First thing you will need to do is open the back of the dryer, with it unplugged, and check the Thermal Fuse. This can be done with a multi-meter or temporarily jump the two connectors/blade terminals and check if the Dryer runs at the correct temp for all cycles. Since I had the dryer taken apart I figured I would clean out the blower fan area and the fan ducting as well as the entire "innards" of the dryer. After temporarily jumping the thermal fuse I found that it had kicked the bucket as the dryer started to work again due to jumping out the fuse. Did I say that this dryer is 20 years old and the original fuse lasted that long? So I decided that since I have the thing open I might as well replace the other 20 Year old electrical components that were back there. These Items included: the Thermal Fuse, Cycling Thermostat, High Limit Dryer Thermostat and Dryer Thermal cut off. Each have their own job and purpose, so don't skimp out and think you can get away with changing the item that has failed, because if that item failed the others will follow. Did I mention my Dryer is 20 years old? As A side note; I also checked the Heating Element and found that one of the coils had warped and contacted/welded itself the the element body, this is what took out the fuse. A pair of needle nose pliers and a steady hand detached the coil and re-positioned the coil in its original shape and placement. My 20 year old dryer, that was a wedding gift to my wife when she married her fist husband now works like a champ!

We suspect the problems people are having with "blow-outs" of the mesh is not understanding what's at play:
There's a LOT of steam pressure (which can be great! Think steam engine, right!?) and it has to go somewhere. Not allowing the steam to pass through the filter will definitely cause blow-outs:
1) The ground should be a looser grind, like drip grind; more like what's in the pre-packs: NOT espresso grind which will pack tight and not allow the steam to a release.
2) Grounds should NOT be packed in: Again that steam needs to be able to flow THROUGH the grinds, not be BLOCKED by them.

4) There are 5 settings: Warm, Lo, Medium, Hi, and Sear. There’s a chart in the Instructions Manual of what each is capable of doing. I found that I only had to use the setting one below the recommended to get the job done.
5) One drawback of this electric cooktop is that it’s Maximum Run time is ONE HOUR. After which you have to let it cool down before using again. It hampers when using for hot pot or if everything you’re cooking takes longer than one hour. Hence, the 4 stars.
6) It is 120 V, 60 Hz, and 1200 W, pretty powerful. Maybe that’s why you can only use it for one hour at a time.
7) One year warranty

My conclusion is that it’s a good electric cooktop for fast cooking under an hour. Good as an extra burner. My son will inherit this when he goes to college. The price is very reasonable.

UPDATE:
Even when the dishwasher was new, the rack never rolled smoothly and it easily derailed.
Customer reviews of the dishwasher warned us about this. They were correct.
I've hated the rack for years until now.

Fast forward to replacing the wheels...here's some advice that's unrelated to this specific (good) product:
As I put the new ones on, I noticed that the wheels were not aligned to each other, the issue being: the metal axles that are part of the rack are out of alignment.

So, I used a long straight edge to check the alignment of the wheels (after putting the new wheels on loosely), then I removed the wheels one at a time so I could bend (slightly) the axles on the rack. I used a small close-fitting hex socket (that just slips over the "axle") along with an extension (to get some leverage) to do the bending.

I checked the vertical alignment of the wheels and also made sure the wheels are not steering in different directions. I aligned both vertical and "toe-in" by bending the rack axles in two directions as need.

After doing this, the rack finally rolls smoothly and easily for the first time ever. Wish I had done this fix years ago!

Perfect fit. Works great, but the thermostat was not the problem. - Changed the thermostat and the fridge STILL did not work right. Frigidaire 10 cuFt top mount freezer. I live in a town with a river and people put docks on it. Years ago they would use styrofoam blocks for dock flotation; big mistake. Styrofoam has pathways between the foam cells which would allow water infiltration. Eventually the foam would become waterlogged and the docks would no longer float. Frigidaire has used this same type of styrofoam in their fridge. Where the temp sensor is mounted is a 5x3x4 inch block of foam that the temp sensor bulb snakes over and it mounted to. Also the drain tube runs through this block. BAD DESIGN. Water leaks down from the freezer and/or frost builds/melts and waterlogs this block of foam causing an ice block which affects the temperature sensor, so then the temp bulb is covered with ICE. THAT is what causes the fridge to not work properly. THE FIX: remove and replace the foam block with closed cell foam. I cut some pieces from Dow blue building foam. fridge works great now. Been running for three months perfectly. FYI: fridge was only three years old and neighbor bought a new one instead of trying to fix it! Crooked repairmen prob wanted $400 to fix!

I didn't need this, but . . . - Lint builds up over the years in the dryer vent and can either start mucking up your drying cycle or even catch fire if it gets too hot. You should clean the duct every 2-3 years as part of your household routine.

I only have a short run of aluminum flex duct feeding to an outside wall, so it would have been just as easy to replace the duct with a new one. If you have a hard pipe that feeds up the walls, however, you really NEED this Deflector Dryer Duct Cleaning Kit or similar.

This solidly-made kit extends up to 12-feet with six soft fiberglass sections tipped with steel threads and a fat, soft brush head. You can just shove it down the duct by hand or use an electric drill to spin clean the duct with a clockwise spin. (NOTE: you MUST use clockwise--counterclockwise will unscrew the sections!) The long, soft fiberglass sections sorta flop sideways all over the place when using a drill, so you might need to slowly feed it in a section at a time. When I finished, I also used a blower to blast out the last of the lingering dust.

NOTE: Don't tear up the package it ships in--just pull out the staples. When finished you can easily repack and store the tough package on the wall.

NOTE 2: You might be able to use this kit to clean refrigerator coils. They also need to be cleaned every 2-3 years for proper operation and cooling efficiency.

This is a solid five-star cleaning kit.

water filter fix - There have been many reviews written stating that filters for the LT1000-PC not fitting.
The issue is that lg has a defect that have not been addressed or recalled leading to consumer's confusion.
This has to do with the 2 groove heads on the refrigerator not aligning properly with the grooves on the filter.
There are many posts on this.
The best one I found is to file down the notches on the side of an old filter using sandpaper or nail filer and marking a line on the side of the filter to help with alignment.
Then we use the old filter to rotate the grooves head counterclockwise to the correct horizontal position of 9 o'clock and 3 o'clock.

After installing this filter, I have noticed a taste improvement compared unfiltered regular tap water.

The ice sticks together and unless you think to stir it around every 5 minutes for a few times, you get lumps of ice instead of individual cubes. If you're just refillng an ice bucket, it's great. If you want to have a good stash of ice in the freezer, not so much. I live alone, so it's perfect or me. For more than 2, maybe 3 people, I think you'd really need something different. Just my opinion; I suppose you could make it work if you don't have any serious ice-eaters. Anyhow I love it. It's certainly paid for itself a few times over already. The one and only flaw, as far as I'm concerned, is that the lid will hit you in the head (if, like me, you get that close) if you bump it when it's open. Annoying, but not a very big deal. It does require cleaning every few weeks. It recommends using vinegar, I assume to discourage mold, so I use a very weak vinegar/water solution, wipe it dry, and there's no taste. It's worked well for me. I don't use the drain plug because it's too much trouble. I just bought a turkey baster to suck most of the last of the water out and a few paper towels. Cleaning takes about 5-10 minutes. No problems so far.
I highly recommend this ice maker for anyone who loves ice or just has no ice maker in their fridge. I don't think you'll ever regret it.

This causes the food to become mixed with the water, and get pumped through the pump and back through the spray arms. Things like Rice and Stickers off of new cups and you name it clog up the arms, EXPECIALLY this center arm. My dishwasher has a lower spinning arm on the bottom of the tub, this one attaches to the underside of the top rack, and then there is the top arm at the top of the dishwasher which is pretty useless. I have taken the arms off at least 50 times and cleaned them by hand in the tub, soaking in vinegar, using pipe cleaners and wire to clear them out. I finally gave up when something got caught inside that I couldn't dislodge. THIS WORKED LIKE A CHARM. However, here is something IMPORTANT FOR ALL TO READ. When you take off the arm under the top rack - KEEP THE SCREW AND WASHER THAT COME OUT. This arm does not have a new replacement screw or washer, and you'll need that to reinstall new arm. This is not a defect or anything - It is just good information to have before you throw out the screw and washer and then have to go digging through the garbage to find it again, clean it and be able to put the new arm on. Also - the part number from GE and the part number for this arm (and pretty much all other arms for dishwashers) do not match. I simply eyeballed the picture and it looked identical and took a chance. It is identical. Works great. Wife is happy. I'll probably end up buying another to pre-plan for the next clog that occurs when my family decides to put a bowl full of rice into the dishwasher without rinsing it out first.

Compact, efficient, well-made! Excellent purchase! - The Giantex mini washing machine is everything I had hoped it would be, and more. This is truly a really mini washing machine with most of the features of a large basic washer. The control panel is simple to use. The load capacity is surprisingly large (one set of twin sheets, or two large bath towels and several wash cloths, or about 7-8 shirts and 4-5 pairs of shorts, or 2-3 pairs of jeans for example). The wash and spin cycles are quick and fairly quiet. The clothes come out clean and spun to a good damp dry. The machine is so light (less than 30 lbs), which makes moving it easy if needed. I bought it to use in a small house we are renting, and it has not disappointed me a bit. It plugs into a standard three-prong grounded outlet and seems to be very energy efficient.
TIPS:
- You will need to purchase a Y-adaptor for the inlet hoses (which I purchased for about $13 at a home improvement store). You cannot select hot, warm, or cold on the machine, so you’ll want to keep your inlet spigots accessible and turn the water on accordingly. I turn them off at the spigot after I’m done washing for the day.
- The water will drain automatically. Our house already had a drain pipe, so we put our outlet hose down in the tube. It has never leaked. The first time I ran it, I did not realize it would drain automatically, just like a full-size washer; so make sure you have it set to drain outside, or into a bucket or sink if needed.
- There is no compartment for adding detergent, so you’ll want to toss in your detergent, fabric softener, bleach, and laundry boosters as the machine fills. I use 1/3 of the detergent I would for a regular machine.

Keep an eye on the filter! - I got one of these for my basement, because it gets really hot and since my game room doubles as my office, it can become sweltering. But if you live in an area of moisture (like a basement, or anywhere on the East Coast), be aware these cooling systems have some limitations.

Here's how it works: you put water in it. It blows air over the water, which is hopefully cold water. It's like continually misting yourself with ice water. That's it, the end. That's the secret to how all these devices work. They're just variants of the same technology.

One innovation with this tool is it shows you how cool it is, which is great (but not necessary, you'll know if it's not working). It also has a filter (curtain) that you wet and put in the freezer, which definitely helps keep things cooler than if you're using water alone. You can even put ice cubes into the receptacle on top.

The downside of these devices is that they're only as good as the amount of water you put in them. You have to bring the device, which is corded, over to the water, or bring the water to the device. This is a pain and prone to spillage. The curtain of frozen water makes a big difference, although you still need to add water to it.

The really big problem with these devices is mold. Over times, blowing air over water encourages mold. The cleaning tray helps somewhat, but if you see black spots on the filter, you're done. The older version I used started to get moldy, and then all I could smell was mold blowing on me, which triggered my allergies.

If you live in a dry, hot climate, this will work quite well. For us basement-dwellers, keep an eye on that filter.

Works well enough but doesn't really stay put. - If you're searching for this, you know what it is. My gas range is the standard 36" range with built-in oven that is found in many homes. Nothing fancy. The problem is that there is a small gap between the range and the cabinet/countertop that food or liquid can fall into.

These Stainless Steel Stove Gap Covers solves exactly this problem. Due to its proximity to the fire and heat, the gap cover must be metal and because will be exposed to oils and other food particles, it needs to be easy-to-clean. These covers fit both criteria.

With an extendable piece, these covers can fit all ranges regardless of the depth of the stove and there is a small metal piece that is supposed to provide tension when inserted into the gap. Unfortunately, this is where I have the first problem with this product. The tension just isn't enough to keep the gap cover in the gap snugly. I think a cork or silicone piece would help give it the friction in needs to stay in place.

The second problem I have is that the product is in the shape of the letter "T" but because there is a slight difference in height between my range and the counter, it has to tilt to one side, further making it hard for the cover to stay in place.

The last issue is the extension part. It doesn't lock into a position. Without it, you can accidentally push on the cover and shorten it. It would be better to have some sort of locking mechanism that will keep it to the length that you set.

You can use these front rollers to replace the back ones on GE dishwashers - In GE dishwashers, this part number WD12X271 is for the front bottom rollers, of which there are 4. However, I found they could be used to replace the harder to obtain (especially as a kit together with the axle/clip) back rollers.

The 2 back rollers, WD12X10267, are narrower and once the center of the wheel and/or the axle wear, they wobble and fall off the track. The wider front rollers each take less load (because there are 4 of them) and don't so readily fall off the track both because they wear less and aren't so narrow.

To stop the back of the rack falling off the track, I moved 2 of the front wheels (WD12X271) to the back and they worked fine. Maybe because they, like the rear rollers, had worn somewhat, they were able to move a little to fit into the slightly tighter body dimension at the back. Once the new WD12X271 axles arrived I replaced the front rollers I had moved. Now the dishwasher has 6 wide lower rollers and the bottom rack moves in and out with no problem at all.

You must use a Vertuo capsule, the instructions tell you to fill at 70%, this will produce a very weak cup of brew. Probably why most reviews for flavor are poor. To brew a true 7.77 oz of coffee, the original capsules are packed with 12.5 grams of fine grounded coffee beans. A 70% fill will result in using 8.75 oz, a single espresso capsule contains 7 grams of coffee and a double espresso capsule contains 10 grams of coffee. The only way you’re going to get the flavor you are accustomed to, is to use the same amount, (weight wise) of grinds (each scoop is about 3 ounces) that the capsule originally came with. Keep in mind that each capsule also has a unique bar code on it. This bar code determines brew cycle time, water temperature, water pressure, and how much water to dispense.
So in a nut shell, have multiple capsules available to test with, make sure to use a fine grind, don’t use an old capsule that has been laying around as mold has already been growing inside the capsule. Clean right after using. I will explore other options

pennies or dimes destroy these pumps quickly but the good news is that minimal tools are needed if you have the skill to open the washer wrapper properly.
Remove two console screws without loosing them as they are very specially prepared for that job.
Unplug the spin lockout electric plug
Mark the orientation and remove the two big green spring clips.
Rotate the wrapper forward while noting how it keys into the base by looking past the lid hole. This is important as it is first time tricky.
Back the wrapper away to reveal the pump
Using long nose locking plier tool move hose clamps back and unplug hoses.
Study how the pump mount clips tag into the motor as this is not immediately clear the first time you do this.
Unclip the two clips and note they will fall away easily.
Pull the old pump off while noting that there are two plastic locating pins that must be in place when you plug in the new pump.
Note the orientation of the flats of the motor drive and align the new pump to match
Re-assemble the machine.

If the washer manufacturers would just put this screen into their designs, it would save millions of hours of wasted time and money for us owners.

A failed pump is one of the most common problems with almost any washing machine. IF they would sell just the pump vanes, I would buy 6 of them to keep on the shelf. Too bad they do not incorporate a course screen in the inlet.

Knobs not compatible with original Jenn-Air KIP-5D09-3/-4/-1 knobs - The knobs sold on Amazon looked almost identical to the ones on my 2003 Jenn Air stove, so I assumed they would fit. They didn't. The original Jenn Air stove knobs have the ID letters/numbers "KIP-5D09-3", or -4, or -1 as the final number on the inside of the knob. The REPLACEMENT knobs have the ID letters/numbers "KIP-5D01-2", or -3 as the final number. Note the originals knobs are 5D09 (NINE!!) and replacements are 5D01 (ONE!) which are a tad too small and do not fit my Jenn Air stove. Therefore, be certain to pre-check the numbers on your knobs to determine if your stove requires the 5D09's OR the 5D01's. Thank you.

The design changed so these no longer fit as designed, I made it work though. - Bosch changed the design of how the tab at the end of this cord connects to the spring which regulates the soft opening of the dishwasher door (our dishwasher is 5-6 years old). This tab doesn't insert into the original plastic clip on the spring, buyer beware. In the end I removed the plastic clip from the spring and simply threaded the new cord through the coils of the spring and used the plastic tab on the end of the cord to act as a stop from pulling through the coil. The tension of the spring coils keeps the tab locked inside the barrel of the spring. For now this solution works, the tension is a bit too tight and I imagine after many uses the spring will "saw" though the cord but after spending all the time pulling out my dishwasher to discover this part is no longer correct I decided to make it work and I did. I noticed that a piece of plastic extended on the back end along the shaft hole, probably from the plastic molding process, so I used needle nose pliers to break it off (about 1/16th of an inch of protruding plastic) and this allowed the wheel to sit properly on the shaft so that the c clip could be installed properly.

I initially thought the dryer belt had gone so I ordered that part and luckily noticed that someone else recommended this part as the reason for the slipping and banging noise. They were correct in that the shaft hole on the old blower wheel had smoothed out and a portion of it had broken, which was preventing the wheel from turning properly and sucking hot air into the dryer. However, the old belt looked like it was starting to fray so it was good to change that as well. I also ordered an extra idler pulley, which probably didn't need to be changed, but I changed it anyway.

If you use "coarse of medium" grind, your coffee will be very weak as they are very granulated and the machine won't have enough time to infuse and remove the coffee flavor from it. overpriced - This is a polyphosphate cartridge. Practically, it cannot "filter" the scale-causing minerals from the water, as there is far too much volume of minerals to hold in the tiny cartridge. Instead, the cartridge releases a small amount of polyphosphates into the water. Those chemicals inhibit the formation of the scale -- in simple terms, they keep the minerals suspended in the water and inhibit them from forming the white deposits. Of course, the minerals have to go somewhere, and they can't stay suspended indefinitely as they won't evaporate as steam. Some of the mineral material inevitably forms scale, while the rest is flushed out of the humidifier tank in the flush cycle (which is frequently problematic on the troublesome TrueSteam humidifiers). So the polyphosphates released by this cartridge help to inhibit scale by keeping the minerals suspended until they get flushed.

Now that you understand how it works, you can go get a standard 1/4" quick-connect, in-line polyphosphate scale-inhibiting filter that's twice the size for half the price. Either way, you can only expect it to last about 6 months. The polyphosphates used in these filters are "food grade" and considered acceptable for whole-house use, including drinking water (although there's no benefit for drinking). Polyphosphates are sometimes used in lieu of water softeners.

Simple Solution For Washer Ventilation - These door stand-off devices are a no-brainer solution to the problem of washer laundry appliances developing mildew smells and helps slow the build-up of mold in the rubber door seals.

To use them it is required your appliance(s) have metal on the face so that the magnet can be attracted for stabilizing the stand-off. In my case the two washers we have a Whirlpool brand, model WFW92HEFUO, that have a stainless steel finish but the magnets still grab on and do their job. Granted this review is being written immediately after installing the two units I bought. The magnetic strength is not especially strong but the magnets in the two units I received definitely have enough power to hold themselves in place and do their intended job. Please note, if your appliance(s) have a stainless steel finish there's a possibility these might not work since not all stainless steels are magnetic.

It's also nice there is a rubber coating on the magnet surface itself which not only prevents it from scratching your appliance but it also gives a bit of a tack to the device which helps prevent it from sliding down from the place you choose to mount it.

Overall these are a very simple solution to a very common problem of mal odor from front-loader laundry washing machines.

99.8595% water - you got me this time - I normally check ingredients because I'm a chemist by education and trade. That said, I blow it sometimes and did so with this as well because I was in a hurry and I ordered it late at night. I could kick myself. According to the label, this is 99.96% water, or 0.14% active ingredient. Now understand that the essentially same active ingredients that are used in swimming pool algaecide, but those are sold at 40-60% active ingredients, making that up to 428 times stronger than this product.

In case you're not good at math, if you buy a quart of 60% pool liquid algaecide that has the words "ammonium chloride" in the name of the active ingredients, you can literally put a half teaspoon of that algaecide in a quart of water and you'll still have something slightly stronger than this garbage. That makes this product roughly 200 times more expensive per quart and means you are buying very little other than a plastic bottle to put in a landfill.

Please, only buy this if you're lazy and can't measure out a half teaspoon of something.

You turn your device on and to whatever setting and press that button and it will turn the device off when done.

I applied a thin layer of base coat to my nail and let it cure for 2 minutes. Then I applied a thin layer of gel polish and let it cure for 2 minutes. I repeated the same step until I got the desired opacity. Afterwards, I touched it softly to see if the polish was dry and noticed it was very slightly still not dry (a light print of my fingerprint) so I put the top coat on and cured for about 5 minutes. It was completely dry by then, as I used thin coats and cured between so that it wasn't completely wet on bottom and dry just on top and smudge. I am very happy with this curing lamp, as it is my first. It is great quality plastic and the bottom of the inside of the lamp slides in/out for your convenience. Right now I'll just put the food in fabric grocery bags and at least that way it is sorted (beef, chicken, vegetables, fish) so I won't have to get in and out of it too often. Do NOT get the 3.5 size, get at least the next size up, 5.0. I didn't because the cost was out of my budget. I'm grateful to have a freezer, don't get me wrong, but had I ordered a month ago, I could have gotten the next size up for $30 less than what I paid for this scrawny freezer. Oh, the weight: 42 pounds, not 48 as listed on the description. The height is about counter height, less than 2 feet wide, less than 2 feet deep. This filter costs more than others, almost double, because it does more than others, much more than double. It is a certified ANSI 53 filter which includes ANSI 42.
[...]

ANSI 42: Establishes the minimum requirements designed to reduce aesthetic or non-health-related contaminants, such as chlorine, taste, odor and particulates. Products are certified only for material safety, pressure bearing and structural integrity, not for filtration capabilities.

ANSI 53: Establishes the minimum requirements for the certification of filtration systems designed to reduce specific health-related contaminants, such as Cryptosporidium, lead, volatile organic chemicals(VOC) and asbestos that may be present in public or private drinking water. The reduction claims are verified by this standard.

Basically, ANSI 42 may make your water taste better, but ANSI 53 is required to make your water safer to drink. What is the purpose of filtration if it does not make the water safer to drink?

There are a couple of differences between this one and many of the others. One is the fact that this one makes ten bullets of ice instead of nine… The other is the fact that this one has a timer so that it will not continue to run at times when you do not need it to, like when you’re sleeping.

The listing shows that this particular icemaker can make up to 33 pounds of ice in a twenty-four hour period. This might be true, but that is only if you continually remove the ice from the basket as it is being made. The ice maker makes the ten bullets of ice… Then place them into a basket. If you do not remove the ice from the basket, then it simply melts and refreeze is. Once the ice is in the basket, the machine will not keep the ice frozen. If you need a lot of ice, then you will need to manually remove the ice from the basket and place it into your own freezer.

This icemaker is made in China and being sold by Chinese coming on Amazon. It works quite well as long as you have the right expectations.

The length of the shaft is about an eighth of an inch shorter than my original, and the entire switch was mounted sideways so OFF would be on top, just as it is on all the three other original switches. I used my laser temperature 'gun' to determine that the LO was the lower temperature and the HI was the higher temperature.

Other than those two points, the switch is a satisfactory replacement for the 30-plus year-old switch which controls the large eight-inch burner. The indicators on the replacement (Frigidaire) switch - L1, L2, H1, H2 and P - all coincide with the indicators on the original (Magic Chef).

UPDATE: Middle of August 2017 and the switch is still functioning as it did when it was first installed. This switch rotates easier than the 30-year-old switches do.

The controls are easy to use, it works quickly, and ejects the ice neatly and properly each time. But, as with any bullet ice machine, the ice itself is not of ideal quality. It's cloudy and melts quicker than clear ice. Clear ice machines do cost a fair amount more (the Frigidaire model is probably the least expensive one but it costs nearly twice as much as this) but the ice quality is better. Still, for the price, this is a good performer in the bullet ice category.

The overall fit and finish is decent. The gearing for the ice ejection is all plastic, but that's to be expected for the price. The manual is pretty poor, but it's not hard to figure out how to use the machine. Operating sounds are hushed (other than the loud bang the ice makes when it is ejected and hits the catch container). It has a self-cleaning function but I can't tell what it actually cleans -- it seems to just recirculate the water a few times. I imagine it is cleaning (or attempting to clean) hard water deposits on the innards of the machine, but can't be sure.

There's a drain plug which is handy for getting rid of the water when you're done with the machine. It is located on the bottom, so you have to position the machine so the front half is hanging over a sink so it can drain without making a mess. Not the most convenient place for a drain plug, but it works.

Although this has all the limitations of other bullet ice machines, it works well and is easy to use. For the price it's a five star performer. If you are willing to spend a bit more, however, it's worth looking at clear ice machines since the ice quality is better.

Sonic ice? Sort of. - I'll get to the "Sonic Ice" part below.

The ice maker required no assembly at all when it came out of the box, but instructions in two places said it needed to sit upright before use so that the refrigerant could settle into place. Instructions plastered to the maker said 24 hours; those in the manual said 1 hour. I let it sit overnight--it was fine.

Instructions suggested cleaning out the maker with warm soapy water, and I'd say that's good advice since I found several hair-like strings of glue around some of the joints. There's a small plug on the underside to drain the water from inside once cleaning is finished.

When the lid is lifted, you look in and see a plastic basket which sits towards the top of the machine in the front half. The ice drops in here when it is formed. (The back half is where the ice makes.) The "water tank" is just the area below the basket, and when you fill it with water, you have to be sure not to let it come up to the bottom of the basket. A pump pulls the water up into the back half of the maker to make the ice, which takes maybe five minutes or so.

HERE"S THE CRUCIAL PART: There is no "freezer" aspect to this maker. Once the ice drops in the basket, it sits there until it melts back into the water tank if you don't use it. I think the maker must monitor the weight of the basket to trigger the mechanism to make more, as it will keep the basket full.

SONIC ICE? Well, sort of. It has a different shape--that hollow bullet shape--but because the maker doesn't store the ice at freezing temperatures, it's 'softer' to chew than ice from a refrigerator freezer.

VERY HAPPY WITH THE PRODUCT! It's quiet, except for those moments when the ice rattles into the basket. We turn it off at night. Keeps my wife in all the ice she can chew!

Convenient Means to Making Ice - We have issues with our ice maker in our refrigerator. It is far too slow to produce ice and we have considered getting another refrigerator because of it. We usually just buy bags of ice to solve the problem, but for convenience sake, I decided to get this Frigidaire ice maker.

Compact in size, this ice maker sits on the countertop and produces just enough ice to make it useful for beverages and other modest needs. You just open the flip top, pour in water, and wait about 10 to 15 minutes for the first batch of cubes of ice to be made. The small cubes are bell/gumdrop shaped and are small enough to fit in tight spaces, making them good for those who want to add ice to, say, water bottles and other receptacles that cannot handle normal sized ice cubes.

The outside of this ice maker has lights that indicate Ice Full, Add Water, and Ice Making. The top two indicators display a red light, to get your attention The one annoyance I have with this ice maker is that the ice tends to stack up in the back, which triggers the sensor and causes the ‘Ice Full’ light to come on. There could, in fact, be plenty of space in the ice bin and you will need to open, pull the ice down from the back, and close to make the ice maker resume. The problem is that the ice is dumped in back and stacks up on the back edge. A change to the engineering- having it dump the ice in the middle of the ice container, for example- would fix this problem.

Other than that, this Frigidaire ice maker works well and produces the necessary ice to use in beverages for my family of four. It takes up little space and you can easily flip open the lid to get the ice you need. It’s a good investment for those who have a faulty ice maker in the fridge and who are tired of making regular trips to the store to purchase bags of ice.

They have Their Issues, but Seem to be Cost Effective - I'm 9 Months into using these Reusable K-Cups and have had varying experiences along the way:

For reference, I have a Kuerig 2.0

I'm the only one who uses these at home, and I use the in pairs: two 6 oz shots, which I read was recommended and can confirm is better than 12 oz through one.

The first two worked well in general.
On one (I'll refer to it as K-Cup #1), the lid broke pretty early: it was still usable, just less convenient.
The mesh started splitting on K-Cup #2 first, but it ended up lasting about as long as #1 (by which I mean that it leaked very few grinds for a long time).
K-cup #3 replaced #2, and my Kuerig didn't want to recognize it immediately: it took several attempts each time to get it to pass.
I experimented with #3, trying to find a pattern: I would spin it to see if orientation mattered and closed the lit with varying speeds and force. Eventually I slammed it hard enough that a chip busted out of the rim surrounding where the needle goes: since then the K-Cup has worked perfectly.
The Kuerig also would not recognize K-Cup #4: I tried my previous method of slamming it at first, thinking that I'd prefer the needle clear what space it needed (and that I'm seriously getting fed up with Kuerigs at this point and am thinking of switching back to traditional brewing methods), but couldn't get the needle to chip this cup. So, I took a knife and carved out some of the plastic rim; the K-cup now works about 75% of the time, which is obviously less often than #3 but is acceptable.

The other thing I have noticed is that the splitting is probably due to packing the K-Cup: at first I was stuffing grinds in there and forcing the lid closed; now I just pour the grinds in and brush the top so that the lid closes easily. This seems to improve the life span of the K-Cups somewhat.

Male to Male Fittings - This is a slick product. We've had trouble with the hose sliding off the vent pipe, so this is a great idea. A couple warnings though:
1) The plastic connectors are both male fittings. If the pipe in your wall is also a male fitting, the plastic coupler will not slide into it, even after you prepared it as in the instructions. And once you've cut it as instructed, it is compromised--and inside the wall. I straightened out the tabs I cut in the pipe and used aluminum duct tape to attach the platic fitting to the pipe in the wall. I'm hoping the adhesive on the tape will hold up under the heat. Otherwise I will need to cut a larger hole in the wall to replace the elbow that I damaged preparing it for the DryerDock fitting.
2) You rotate the two pieces together to attach. There's not a lot of friction holding them in place (they don't truely "lock"). If there's much spring force to twist them back counter-clockwise, they will come apart. I'm planning to drill a hole through the two to insert a pin & thus lock them in place.

Docking (no pun intended) one star because the instructions could have warned about pipe fitting incompatibilities & the locking mechanism could be better.

All that being said, I'm planning on buying a second DryerDock to put on the dryer side of the hose, as the hose tends to slide off there too. The dryer side connector also looks to be male, so I'm going to check at a hardware store for a short slip fitting to join the two male ends.

Infinite Range Switch Desmystified Right Here! - Works perfect as a replacement to a similar looking stove switch on my smooth top stove. I didn't need one of the connections. Basically if your current switch has H1, H2, L1, L2, P, connections and the wattage reads 2100-2600w or 8.9-11.0A (amps) then this is the one for you. I had the large burner and there was a LOW connection (L1 I think) that I did not need to hook to. I suspect you may be able to use the same switch for a small burner and would likely not use one the of the HIGH connections. BUT if you have the large burner DON'T buy one that says 1250-1560W (watts) or 4.4-7.4A (amps). That is lower power than you will need. When hooking up the new one don't worry about the wire color, order or location since they vary in front vs. rear burner and brand to brand. Just copy the wire locations of your old switch to the new one: H1 to H1, L1 to L1, P to P, etc.. the spade locations and look of the switch were a bit different from stock but it works perfect and temperature is the same as the other large burner I measured with my digital thermometer. It is also possible the screw threads that hold it to the metal panel could also vary from what you have and it does not come with screws, I don't think any others do either. I lost my original switch screws anyway and I have a large screw jar so this was no biggie for me. If you need to replace the screws just use ones barely long enough to grab the front of the switch and not go deep in or you may ruin the switch or touch a contact. I hope this helps someone. I was overly worried about wire colors and switch shape, etc. It's ALL about wattage, connections (H1, L1) and the shaft that your knob slides onto. Match those and your good. FORGET brand loyalty. Frigidaire, Kenmore, Hotpoint, GE, Whirlpool, Amana, Electrolux, etc are all in bed together. Chances are your $2,000 GE 6 burner Profile stove has the same switch as the $449 Whirlpool apartment grade one.

The only way you can continually make and save nice is if you remove the basket, about once per hour, and place the ice into a receptacle and place it in your freezer.

For those unaware Whirlpool has purchased Maytag animana and is now manufacturing the replacement parts for these units so you will find multiple part numbers weather there are a Whirlpool number a Maytag number or an Amana number that are all the exact same part. For example, this part was sold under Whirlpool part wpy 54414 but it's also listed as part# AP6024203(likely the AP stands for Amana even though the product is a Maytag).
This machine is over a decade old and the only repairs it's required so far was a new belt a few year back and now this pully wheel. We decided to replace the belt (part# wp40111201 AKA part # AP6009126) while we were in there as it had some cracks starting and we might as well save ourselves the hassle.
The pully did NOT come with either the washer or microscopic retaining clip but that's okay as our old ones were still in great condition.
It also doesn't come with installation instructions (super simple, washer threaded onto post of idler arm, add pully wheel, second washer, and then retaining clip) for the pulley itself or how the belt should be rethreaded onto the pulley wheel or the motor mount. YouTube will be your friend for putting the belt on properly, check multiple videos to find the one that works best for you.
This repair was relatively quick (for a gas unit you will be doing the threading blind, check youtube to see what I mean) and seems to have resolved the issues.
Just remember, always unplug your electrical connections and in the case of gas dryers like ours, simply shut off the natural gas valve at the back of the until as well until the repair is completed.

Convenient for folks who use a lot of ice - There are already two excellent video reviews of this maker, so I am going to fill in the cracks and try not to repeat the product specs or what has already been said. Like the two other reviewers I received my maker as a review sample.

Operationally this is fairly economical since it draws about two hundred Watts (two old style light bulbs.) I do want to set expectations. This will absolutely produce the claimed 26.5 pounds of ice in a twenty-four hour period, but not all at once. Per cycle it will produce a little less than two pounds. A cycle takes up to twenty plus minutes, depending on the ice size that you select. The smaller ice is made a little faster than the largest of the three different 'cube' sizes. Moreover, this will only store a single cycle's worth of cubes, so if you are using it at a party it will require some management of the completed cubes as well as refilling the maker (it takes 2.8 liters of water per cycle.)

The unit is compact and has a few basic operating requirements, like ensuring that the side vents are not blocked. Also, it is not designed for outdoors use, so factor that in if you are purchasing this for a pool party or BBQ.

What it does do, though, is efficiently product ice on a nearly continuous basis as long as you manually transfer the finished ice to insulated coolers as well as keep the reservoir filled between cycles. In that respect the performance is very impressive, and each load of ice is substantial. I am estimating that one of these can easily keep a party of twenty supplied in ice for drinks. Plus, when you factor in the low energy consumption that I cited above this makes an excellent personal ice maker.

Perfect for my chicken coop! - I’m in Alaska and temps have been -17 F every day for 2 weeks, and it’s only mid-November. With 2 1/2 - 3 months of temperatures like this, my chicken would have serious frostbite and maybe even die, without some heat even in their insulated coop.

We put a radiant oil heater in the coop and use this Inkbird temperature controller to keep the heat at 34 degrees at roost level.
The controller turns the electricity that runs the heater on at 33 degrees, and off at 35. The coop temp has been very consistent and gives me peace of mind.
The floor of the coop is colder so the chickens are still acclimated to below freezing temps, but they get to rest and sleep above freezing which puts less stress in them.

The set up was a little confusing, it helped to read the reviews here to understand what PV, SV, etc meant.
Basically, set the temp for the highest you want it to go which is where you will want the heat to turn off.
Then set the differential to the number of degrees you want the heat to kick on: I set mine at 35 a the max heat I want and where the electricity will kick off. I set the differential at 2, which is 2 degrees less than my max heat of 35. This means the electric will turn on when the coop is at at 33 degrees, and will cut off when the coop temp reaches 35 degrees.

I am very happy with this unit.

The stock board for the fridge has a default state of ON. Power goes off, power goes on, and the stock board turns your fridge back on, like it's supposed to.

You'll have enough ice for a drink or two in that time, sure, but expect to run this machine for 6 hours non-stop if you need a gallon of ice.

Here is what you can expect ( tested on Large Ice setting ):

1. One complete cycle creates 1 quart ( 4 cups ) of ice
2. Once complete cycle takes just over 90 MINUTES to complete
3. There are 10 batches of ice per cycle, with each batch taking between 9-10 minutes.

Expensive but heavy duty paper type product - Chemex has a couple of these white coffee filters on the market; this one lists around 11 bucks; there is an almost identical one that lists at 9 bucks through Amazon too. I have both products (wanted to see what the difference was). I don't see any major (or minor) differences, so first, buy the cheaper one (my advice). As to the product, they really are much heavier than the typical coffee filters you buy--even the "better" brands. One thing though, these are kind of weird. You get them, and they are folded in four sections. You can use them on a regular coffee machine (cone type), but they are specifically designed for the glass chemex glass decanters. What's strange is you are directed to unfold one portion (of the folded pieces) and put the other three sides toward the decanter pouring opening. In essence you have three sides touching the glass on one side and one side touching the glass on the other side where is all fits into the cone (or rounded opening). So why have three sides to filter when the other side is just one layer thick? It's hard to explain, and other reviewers have tried; don't let that discourage you though, it really is a great product, and it (these heavy filters) is the main reason Chemex glass decanters produce such superior coffee (well, that plus the fact that you control the temperature of the water going through your coffee grounds). Hope this helps. Update: The difference between the FC-100 and the FS-100 is this one is a CONE and the other one is just a sheet of paper folded into quarters (a reqular sheet of paper folded twice). The cone fits a little better into the Chemex in my opinion. Prices fluctuate, so keep that in mind.

Get a transparent hose for easier drainage troubleshooting - I have done a lot of dishwasher troubleshooting as a manager of rental properties. Most dishwasher drain hoses I encounter are somewhat transparent. I can see water and debris flowing through them and can see accumulated debris. This is useful when troubleshooting a drainage issue or investigating a possible clog. While not essential, since transparent hoses are so readily available, why not get one of those instead of this opaque one? The transparent ones are the hazy white-colored one that allows light through. For the prior drainage issue I dealt with I was able to see the clog in the drainage hose, which I would not have been able to do if this opaque hose was installed.

Fits into LG LFXS30766S - My LG LFXS30766S refrigerator was icing up in the refrigerator compartment behind the bottom drawer. One symptom was that the drain hole iced over, so when the defrost the water could not get into the bottom evaporator pan and I would have pooled water in the refrigerator, where it would eventually freeze.

I initially solved the clogging issue with a short copper wire. I had some scraps of electrical wire that I stripped off the coating and wrapped it around the defrost line and had the wire extend down into the drain hole. A YouTube video shows how this works. The concept is the defrost line heats up and the heat extends to the copper wire in the drain hole. This copper wire trick worked.

While searching for a solution I came across these drain clips and I figured they would work even better due to the larger surface area. The next time I had to work on my refrigerator I pushed the copper wire aside and attached this clip. I had to bend the tip so the tip was not touching the plastic drain tube. These are made for a Samsung, but they work fine in an LG, and are easier to install than a copper wire because the clip right to the defrost line instead of having to be wrapped around with pliers. I bought two of these in case I have to install the same thing in the freezer compartment, or in case I need to solve this same problem in another refrigerator.

An earlier clog with similar symptoms was caused by hard water deposits clogging the bottom of the drain tube, where it touches the evaporator pan in the back. I fixed this by cutting off the bottom of the drain tube to leave a gap between the drain tube and the pan.

My refrigerator was still icing over after the copper wire fix, although the problem of water not draining was addressed. I am swapping a replacement defrost sensor next to see if that helps, which is why I had the back off to install this drain clip.

Use screws and attach firmly. This will prevent hoses from coming undone. I have horizontal sliding windows but height of window was greater than length of the pieces that fir in there so had to make an extension, but it is easy. Attach the bottom hose from the window to the intake side of the AC and the discharge should go to upper hole. Heat rises. This is my first portable ac, and if you need a portable, this isn't too bad and has dual hoses, so that is a plus. The unit is fairly noisy, but aren't they all. The fan..even on low, blows pretty hard, but cooling is good. Cooling won't be the same for each user, as more than likely room to be cooled might/might not be insulated, and therefore allows more heat to come in regardless. The ac unit does put out plenty of cool air. How your room absorbs it will depend on your room. Overall, at the price I paid, this is a good unit with dual hoses which is a plus. I wrapped the discharge hose loosely with tin foil and this prevents much heat from leaking from the hose walls into the room you are trying to cool. I do not think any of these portable units work quite as good as a window unit and these portable units are certainly take more space up in your room. Happy cooling. I will come back if there are issues, but so far, this unit works quite well.

Best Out There - The best thing about these filters is you can fill them with loose leave tea, shake them on the counter, and NOT see a bunch of fine tea particles and dust on your counter (like you can with most any other product). That also means they don't release these particles into the tea water itself, and as a result you don't have to use a strainer.

The mesh on these is like the goldtone filter used for coffee makers since the 1980s or so. They keep particles out of the water.

What I'd like to see to make these better is hinged "wings" that flip up so the filters can be used over wider tea pots.

As it is, I need to buy both sizes depending on the opening of my various tea pots. If they had "wings" that flipped up until they were horizontal I wouldn't have to do that.

At any rate, they work great and it's great to not have to use a strainer when pouring tea.

These are currently the only tea strainers Grace Teas and Mark T. Wendell (where Julia Child bought her tea) offer for sale, and I'm sured they've tried just about every design out there before settling on these.

These are also much easier to clean up after using because the mesh is so fine particles don't get stuck in the mesh the way they do with tea balls.

The product could be improved with wings so it can be used in even wider opening tea pots,, and there's no need to use the lid when using in a tea pot (use the pot's lid instead), but other than that, there's nothing that performs better at keeping dust and fine particles off your counters and out of your water. Highly recommended.

The aftermarket 'saves you money' filter pushed a component in the filter attachment into a position where it doesn't allow any water at all to be filtered. The amount saved by using one Waterdrop filter ended up costing almost a grand - GE only replacement part, a diagnosis visit, and then a repair visit. Why so much?

The refrigerator is seven foot tall, forty-two inches wide, and nearly five hundred pounds empty, so the repair requires two appliance repair technicians to remove it from the cabinet so they can drill out the rivets - no simple screws here- panels from the back of the refrigerator, install a very expensive GE only part, re-rivet the rear panels into place, and do a 'fair' job re-caulking the interior panels that needed to be removed.

Comments based on some of the other reviews: Less filtering means quicker glass refills- but is it consistent over the life of the filter? I have the extra couple of seconds for cleaner water. The data shared by both manufacturers is right there for even the cheapest, ahem, 'financially efficient,' health conscious user to see.

Issue: Dish washer was filling and draining twice in a night. Samsung did some engineering and saved my house from flooding with water by turning on the drain pup automatically because of the old part failing to stop the inflow of water.

My way of install: There might be an easier way but... I disconnected power, water inlet, drain hose and removed the lose items inside of the washer. I then pulled the dishwasher out of the cabinet and put it on its back watching for any water leaking. Removed the front white cover plate behind the kick plate. Lifted straight forward on the circuit board back hosing. Then removed the two screws from each side of the plate behind where the electrical box was. Detached the white barbed connectors from the inside kick plate and rolled it forward and out. Unscrewed the inlet valve 90 degree brass fitting to reuse it on new part and then removed 3 screws holding valve in. Went to the mid left side and used needle nose pliers to move hose clamp and disconnected the 13mm ish black hose from the clear plastics part . Then was able to bring valve and hose forward enough to unhook electrical connector from inlet valve. Reused the black hose on new part. Reassembly was the reverse. I tightened the 90 degree brass fitting onto the new valve once the valve was screwed back into the washer so as to not fidget with the lose part. Of note the inner kick panel was a pain to get back in and reattached to the white barbed wire loom retainer. It took me about 30 to 45 minutes to get out fixed and back into the cabinet. Needle nose pliers, 2 screwdrivers, crescent wrench, pipe thread tape and 40 years of fixing stuff around the house.

Saved me from buying a new fridge. - Our 1994 Kenmore refrigerator quit cooling. I could hear it try to start but it would immediately shut back down. I recognized this as a symptom of a bad starter relay. Unfortunately the OEM part is obsolete. I ordered one of these starers and wired it in (very simple). The refrigerator started right up and has been running fine since.

If this happens to you and the OEM part is still available for your refrigerator it's better to use the original part (complicated engineering reason). But if you find yourself in my situation with no option other than buying a whole new refrigerator these work great. In fact, I'm buying another one just to have in case of an emergency so I don't lose food because of a refrigerator or freezer failure.

Keep in mind if you are thinking of buying one of these that they come with different capacities based on the size of the compressor you're trying to start. Also, more modern refrigerators or freezers use a run capacitor so they may require a model different from this one. Do your homework before ordering. On second thought if you don't know these things maybe you shouldn't be doing this.

If I could, I would get something else - Had to replace the dishwasher in a new house. Looked into many models, and decided to go with this model (bought at a local BestBuy). Used for 5 months prior to writing this review.

Pros:
1. Washes dishes well.
2. Supposedly saves water (not sure if I can check this claim, so I am taking it as is)
3. Supposedly saves energy cause it's not using dry-heat at the end of the cycle but rather FINISH rinse agent (more on it in #3 of Cons)
4. Nice looks and easy to operate. Mainly use the AUTO wash - set it and forget it. Also we use 3hr delay so we don't get bothered with noise (later about the noise).

Cons:
1. It is much smaller than other dishwashers we have owned and/or operated (primarily Kenmoore and Whirlpool). I think this Bosch's basic model was made smaller on purpose to make you buy a more advanced washer that is sized properly. For a family of 3, we turn the dishwasher on at least every other day, sometomes daily (when we have guests and such)
2. Maybe I got a defective dishwasher, but mine is NOT QUITE. Again, I compare with kenmoores and whirlpools that I have used and/or owned. We set the 3-hr delay so that in the evening we can watch the TV in the living room without having to turn the volume up.
3. This dishwasher goes though FINISH [[ASIN:B0026WRHK6 Finish Jet-dry Rinse Agent, Original Liquid, 32 Oz]] lightning fast. We set the use of FINISH to the lowest, but the LOW indicator lights up every three or so weeks. Maybe the dishwasher is saving water (see #2 in pros above) and energy (see #3 in pros above), but last time I checked water is much cheaper than FINISH liquid. With Kenmoore, we had to refill the liquid no often than once every 3-4 months.

All things considered, we aren't getting anymore BOSCHs. Next time around I am getting a Kenmoore from Sears. They all are regular sizes and don't consume FINISH at lightning speeds.

Easy to install - If the start switch on your compactor is broken, and this is the correct part for your model, go for it. Very easy install on my Whirlpool GX900QPLB0

1. Unplug compactor, or turn off at breaker but make sure power is OFF
2. Open compactor drawer
3. Remove 2 screws under the control panel
4. Lift control panel up slightly, then off
5. Mark the cables so you know where they reattach on new switch, or do what I did and take a pic with your phone
6. Remove the cables from old switch
7. Attach to new switch
8. Slide control panel back into place
9. Replace two screws under control panel
10.Plug compactor in, or turn on breaker

That's it!

Maybe a little too "durable" - These splash shields look and fit exactly like the factory originals. The only problem I've had is that they seem to be stiffer than the original version. This is an issue because of the flawed design of the bottom rack in the Whirlpool/Maytag/etc. dishwasher where the rollers press down on the splash shields when the rack is rolled in and out to load/unload. This pressure seems to be why these splash shields fail so often. Since these don't flex as well as the originals, they are prone to be dislodged when the rack rolls over them. My washer conked out and the new one was about a month in coming. This item in the meantime is great. Here's a summary of the best tips:
This is a small appliance, someone described it like a blender. It is Not a washer replacement, so change that perception or you'll be disappointed.
Fill it to the lowest line load. The second line makes no sense. Water will spill out, even on the gentle cycle.
Don't fill it up. Clothes need to be able to move with water around them. I might do an adult wool blend sweater and a couple pairs of socks, but not jeans and a sweater: too much material for the appliance to handle well.
Make sure the bucket sits properly on the motor and is against a wall or something. This will prevent the bucket spinning. The weight of clothes and water should provide support as well.
Use a tiny amount of detergent. I'm amazed at how clean and nice smelling the clothes are after washing in this thing. What have I been doing up to this point?
Run a rinse cycle when desired. Works great with liquid fabric softener.
Dump out water, squeeze clothes, hang up or throw 'em in a dryer.
I wipe the washer down underneath-to prevent rust I saw in some pictures-and unplug it if I'm not using it for a while.
So full marks and a high recommendation. It isn't as pretty as some of the other washers, but it does the job and that's why I bought it.

The most difficult part was getting pliers on the spring clip that held the rubber hose on. There just isn't enough space to work and not enough hose to pull it out to work on it.
Things to keep in mind... You will need the elbow bracket from the old part. When you remove it, clean off all the old teflon and put 3 or so wraps of new teflon tape on the threads. Tighten that sucker down pretty tight to avoid leaks and make sure the elbow ends up in a useable spot to connect the water line to. You don't want to have to back it off once you tighten it. Put the elbow bracket on before you install the new valve, it's way easier.
As other have mentioned, there is one issue. The 2 screw holes for mount this are not threaded. Do yourself a favor and pre-thread them before you install it. You can use the screws that came off the old part, or, you can tap them with a tap if you have one the correct thread size.

Lightweight Electric Stovetop - This is a fairly lightweight and portable electric cooking stove that plugs into any ordinary household outlet. It's lightweight construction has positives and negatives. It is light and easy to move around for when you aren't using it, but it also does not support very large pots/pans. So, if you think that you are going to be able to put a tea kettle on one burner and a full-sized skillet on the other burner you can forget about it. The heating elements are way too close together for large pots or pans, so you can only use one that is full-sized at a time.

The heating elements themselves are fairly small, so if you are trying to heat a large skillet it will only get to full temperature towards the center. For those of you who don't know the difference between a full-sized electric stove and one of these portable units you should keep in mind that most electric ovens with burners are directly connected to a dedicated 220V circuit, which gives them FAR more energy than a standard 110V power outlet. The result is that neither of the burners gets anywhere near as hot as the heating coils on an electric oven. Water takes longer to boil. Food takes longer to cook. So, be sure to allow for more cooking time than you normally would with an electric oven.

Despite its limitations, for its current price of around $23 this portable electric stove is a bargain. It's something that can easily be dragged into the back yard for BBQs or for plugging in anywhere outdoors. It is not perfect for every situation, but for some situations it works perfectly.

Go to that Tube channel and research and then buy every replaceable item while you got her open. - My 20 year old dryer decided that it was going to heat at it's hottest setting to the point of scalding my hands when removing the clothes from the dryer and causing a major case of wrinkles in my work Polo's. After going to YouTube to find out how to diagnose the issue, I found that there are a few things to check. First thing you will need to do is open the back of the dryer, with it unplugged, and check the Thermal Fuse. This can be done with a multi-meter or temporarily jump the two connectors/blade terminals and check if the Dryer runs at the correct temp for all cycles. Since I had the dryer taken apart I figured I would clean out the blower fan area and the fan ducting as well as the entire "innards" of the dryer. After temporarily jumping the thermal fuse I found that it had kicked the bucket as the dryer started to work again due to jumping out the fuse. Did I say that this dryer is 20 years old and the original fuse lasted that long? So I decided that since I have the thing open I might as well replace the other 20 Year old electrical components that were back there. These Items included: the Thermal Fuse, Cycling Thermostat, High Limit Dryer Thermostat and Dryer Thermal cut off. Each have their own job and purpose, so don't skimp out and think you can get away with changing the item that has failed, because if that item failed the others will follow. Did I mention my Dryer is 20 years old? As A side note; I also checked the Heating Element and found that one of the coils had warped and contacted/welded itself the the element body, this is what took out the fuse. A pair of needle nose pliers and a steady hand detached the coil and re-positioned the coil in its original shape and placement. My 20 year old dryer, that was a wedding gift to my wife when she married her fist husband now works like a champ!

ONE PROBLEM

THE BOTTOM LINE
For a less expensive frother that is lightweight and spins well, this is a decent choice. It has a few improvements that would make me like it better, but it is decent.

MY RATING
Three stars. This just is not as solid or nice as Cafe Casa is. It is better than some other frothers I have used anyway, so for that I give it the three- more like three and a half.

I just did a few loads with the Wonderwash and am satisfied with it - I am a student who lives in an apartment without washer/dryer and don't have a car to go to the laundromat. I just did a few loads with the Wonderwash and am satisfied with it. The assembly is easy, the size of the item is both sufficiently small to be used on a kitchen top yet big enough to wash a few days worth of laundry.

Make sure you put the Wonderwash on a wet surface so that the suction pad can maintain the item while spinning. Also, do not start cracking it too fast too soon, build up the speed gradually.

Personally, I put the detergent first, then fill the Wonderwash half with hot water, add the clothes and give a few spins to pre treat. After 5-10 mins, I start spinning continually for 10 mins. It is not hard to do, when the movement is started you barely feel the weight. Once again, make sure your suction pads will hold it in place. The cap does not leak and the tube provided to drain the water is very efficient.

So far, the only real con is that when you are done, the clothes are so wet, you have to hang them above a tub for a few hours before they are fully drained.

Made in China. Know what to expect before purchasing. - I’ve used several similar ice machines. There are several things you need to know before you purchase this machine to make sure your expectations meet exactly what this machine offers.

First of all, this machine is not connected to water. You fill the reservoir, in the front. Once the water is low, you refill the reservoir.

The listing shows that this machine can make 33# of ice in a 24-hour period. That is only possible if you have someone removing the ice from the basket . . . 24-hous. . . day-and-night.

This machine does not keep the ice frozen. The ice empties into a basket in the front. If you do not remove the ice; it will melt and refreeze. If you want to keep the ice frozen, you must remove it from the basket. . . place it into a plastic bag or container. . .and place it into your freezer. Note that the ice will be “wet” so when you remove it from the freezer, you’ll need to break it apart.

You should turn the machine off when not in use. Such as nights. Otherwise the machine will continue to make ice. . . the ice melts. . . and recycles making ice again and again.

When you clean the machine, you need to add some coffee machine cleaner powder (the type which is mostly citric acid). I use a bottle brush to clean the inside the best that I can. When you start the cleaning cycle, it will run the solution through the machine several times. You need to make sure you use fresh clean water and let it cycle a few times also.

This ice machine is Made in China and being sold by a Chinese company on Amazon. This machine makes 24 small cubes at a time. Other, similar machines, are offered which make nice cubes for under a hundred bucks. Some also have a timer so they turn-off at night.

Well Engineered & Good Output - It took a bit of trial and error, but, I got the machine working well. Instructions could have been a lot clearer.
Water is poured into a reservoir that holds about 1 1/2 liters. The machine produces a "rack" of ice about every 15 minutes. Four cycles will fill the catch box holding the ice. This needs to be emptied after 20 minutes or so since the ice will begin to melt as if it were in a refrigerator. The melt drains off and recycles through the machine so it is not a problem if one doesn't mind smaller ice cubes; they are small to begin with.

The machine works by water flowing from a horizontal tube with many very small holes that allow water to flow over the ice-making rack. It is obvious that the water put into the reservoir must be scrupulously clean. I currently use only filtered water. I think this is essential to prevent a breakdown.

The size of the cubes does vary and can be adjusted. Some people put the fresh ice into bags before putting the ice in a freezer. This is helpful since the fresh ice will "clot" and need to be separated somewhat. I use a wood mallet for the purpose. If the ice is placed into a plastic bag just dropping it on a counter should work to separate the ice.

The making of ice is quite noisy. If I am in the same room as the machine, it sounds like a truck going by.

I am impressed so far. Fridgedaire put a lot of thought into the machine. Cheaper versions of ice-makers have a high rate of negative reviews while Fridigaire has good reviews overall. You will pay for that— It's worth it.

Worked like a charm! - This dryer duct cleaner was about as easy to use and worked as well as you could ask for. The segments are flexible enough to bend around 90 degree corners no problem, though it did take a little bit of finessing to get it around an S-bend in my duct. The kit seems pretty durable, and I don't forsee any issues getting several annual cleanings. 12' was not quite long enough to get my whole duct, but working from each end using a shop vac to assist (see below) took me all of maybe 20 minutes once I got the dryer moved.

In addition to following the instructions about removing the outside vent cap, I found it worked well to stick the blower hose of my shop vac into the dryer end of the duct and blow air through the duct as I worked the rotary brush through. (Just make sure to use a rag or blanket to seal up the end you're working from, so the air is actually forced through the duct) With the shop vac going, and working about 12" at a time, I ended up with a pretty good pile of lint outside that had been cleaned out!

The instructions say to wrap each joint with a piece of duct tape--that's probably a good idea, but as long as you're careful to ONLY rotate the brush clockwise, you will actually be tightening the threaded joints. Another reviewer mentioned setting the clutch on your electric drill to the lowest setting--also a very good idea, just in case the brush were to get caught on a sharp edge of duct or something.

First, you need to be absolutely sure that your frig is out of warranty (yes, this is the one time you should have purchased that extened warranty). Be sure the installed unit is completely deforsted using the force defrost mode or shut ot down for 24 hours. Ensure the ice make is completely free of ice. Remove the harness trim and disconnect the wiring harness. You then need to remove the set screw and detent tab to drop down the bottom half of the component. If this doesn't make any sense to you stop here and call a professional. If you're tracking thus far carefully pull down the lower half and depress the upper tab to free the unit, then slide the ice maker out from around the coil (if you damage this coil just push you refrigerator to the curb for trash pick up, because it'll cost more to fix it than to buy another one). If you manage to get this far, use some food grade silicone to seal up the comparment as this is most likely why you ice make compartment frosted up and damaged your ice maker (there are some youtube videos for this). Next install the new ice maker ensuring that the pads between the halves are aligned with the coil. Close everything back up. If this is outside your wheel house just pay the repairman their blood money. If they properly seal the compartment and don't damage anything during the installation of the new ice maker you shouldn't have any problems with your frig for a long time. Keep in mind that Samsung doesn't own the rights to bad ice make designs as the ice maker is usually the thing that causes the most problems for every brand.
