Almost perfect - tricks to getting a better cup - The number one problem with K cups other than paying $60 per pound for coffee is that you either have to buy the variety packs and figure out what to do with that one version you really don't like, or you have to make a choice to buy a whole box of this or that or have multiple big boxes of brew laying about. Right now, I have 3 Costco size cases of various cups taking up about 4 cubic feet of my house.

So I got these very bright orange things with the idea that I could cut my coffee cost by 90% AND only buy the coffee I want without having to dedicate an entire closet to it.

I was a little concerned as they tend to look a bit flimsy. That however, is not a problem. I've used these now for several weeks and they are actually pretty sturdy. I figure I should be able to get a fair amount of wear out of them and the price wasn't hard to swallow either.

To use these takes a bit of a couple tricks, but nothing hard or time consuming, and once done, you set it and forget it. The first thing is to pull the Kcup holder out of the coffee pot. Open up the top, grab ahold of the holder, and just pull. It comes out and can easily go right back in.

Second, you may find your first cup leaks a bit, so try it first with just hot water. If so, open up the lid and pull down the O-ring just a hair or two. This seals the top of the place where the water goes in. Be careful though because the tip is just as sharp as it looks. Once pulled down, it will stay down unless you go back to the original Kcup, in which case you'll have to adjust it again. Simple!

Why orange? I don't know, but perhaps cheaper plastic? Or I'll suggest a more likely result of helping them not to be lost on a kitchen counter. Look around and these things will just pop right out at you.

It's a nice little invention and I think I'll include one for each of my Kcup drinking offspring at Christmas time.

Made in China. Make sure your expectations meet what the machine will do. - There are a plethora of the small ice machines being sold by Chinese companies on Amazon right now. One of the main differences between them is the number of cubes made at a time. This one makes twenty-four cubes at a time. A lot of the smaller machines make only nine cubes at a time.

This shows that this machine can make 40 pounds of ice in a twenty-four hour period. That’s a little bit misleading, because the only way it can do that is if you continuously remove the ice as it is being made. Once ice is made it goes into a basket and then it starts to melt. The water goes in the bottom and then it is recycled and made back in the ice again. So if you do not remove the ice as it is being made then it simply goes from water to ice to water to ice to water to ice and so on. Also, if you remove the ice and place it into the freezer, the ice will be “wet” so it will freeze together and you will need to break it apart to use it.

This is a nice ice machine, but you just have to make sure that your expectations meet what the machine will do.

This ice machine is made in China and being sold by Chinese company on Amazon.

French Press works better - I was so excited to use this for cold brew since I love so many OXO products, but this was a disappointment. I’ve been making cold brew in a French press until now, and I have been pleased with the results, but since it requires hands on filtering, I thought this OXO system would simplify the filtering and allow the machine to do most of the work. Wrong.
With a French Press, once the coffee has brewed, I can press the coffee and separate most of the grounds from the cold brew. Then I slowly pour it out into a mesh filter lined with a paper filter and wait for it to slowly seep through. I have to change the paper filter half way through before pouring the second half.
With this OXO system, you are supposed to be able to flip the switch and the cold brew will drip down in to the glass carafe below. But the grounds kept clogging the filter and then absolutely no liquid could get through. (I will also note that I have a quality conical burr grinder, so the grind should not be an issue.) I had to stand over it for about 15 min scraping the grounds to the side or scooping spoonfuls of grounds out of the brewing container. After 15 minutes of this, we were left with roughly 2/3 of the volume of cold brew we would have gotten from the same recipe in a French press. The reduced volume was partially due to me scooping grounds out of the way and throwing them in the sink, and partially because there was no way to effectively press the liquid out of the grounds. Also the taste was inferior. Again probably because the most concentrated cold brew couldn’t be pressed out of the grounds.
Overall the taste was nowhere as good and the process was more cumbersome than a French press. I wish I loved this machine, but on the plus side, it’s one less thing to sit on my counter and take up more space in the fridge.

Works better that most - Over the years I've tried a number of the reusable K-cup gizmos and had come to the conclusion that none of them were designed right. None of the companies making these things seem to take in account that the water actually needs to be in contact with the coffee for some period of time to make a decent cup of coffee. If you take a look at a used k-cup, you'll see that there is a small hole in the top where the water goes in and a small hole in the bottom where the coffee comes out. Most of these filter units have large screened opening that don't allow any pressure to build up like a real k-cup does. So you end up with a very weak cup of coffee even if you over pack the filter.

But the design of this Keuring My K-Cup filter is different, it actually takes the place of the whole coffee unit. You can actually get a drinkable cup of coffee from it, even without using a ton of grounds. The one thing I still don't like is having to clean out the basket after every cup. So I've been using these - [[ASIN:B00BUFGMDI Disposable Filters for Use in Keurig® Brewers - Simple Cups - 50 Replacement Filters - Use Your Own Coffee in K-cups]]. They make the chore a bit more palpable.

I might note that I'm using this filter with a Mr. Coffee brand k-cup machine and had no problems installing it. Something else that might be of interest. I purchased the filter I'm using at the local big-box store and paid nearly twice what they want for one here (doh!).

So Far So Good - So the original gasket was ripping inside the dryer and after watching several YouTube videos I decided to try to attempt this myself. Took some binder clips from my office supply stash and clipped it in place on one edge and then started working my way around adding a binder clip every few inches. The glue has quite a strong smell to it so if you are bothered by scents you might want to have someone else do this or make sure you are in a very well ventilated place. The glue is also very runny. I had a few drips but found applying it with Beth drum on it's side like it is positioned in the dryer was helpful to get the glue to run along the bead where you wanted the glue to be anyway. I had to add some extra glue to a few places after the 24 hour cure because it didn't feel like it held in a few spot which may have been application error on my part. I let that cure for 24 hours afterwards and then put the dryer back together. It's gone through a few cycles and so far it seems to be working great and holding up. I will say be prepared because I partially dismantled my entire dryer to make this repair. It isn't hard, but just be prepared. I hope your laundry room is larger than mine. Worked great for a Whirlpool Duet Sport dryer I bought in 2007 - Simple to install. On the inside of the door on a Duet Sport you'll see 3 kinds of screws - one is Torx ('star' bit) and the other 2 are Phillips heads that are different sizes. Remove the 6 smaller ones - one 12 o'clock, two each at 3 and 9 o'clock, one at 6 o'clock. Do yourself a favor and remove the top one last. I use some diagonal cutters to cut the old one so it could come out. press the new one in. Reinstall the screws starting with the top one - leave them loose until all the screws are in. Give the front a jiggle and it will self-align. Tighten the screws - they don't have to be super tight, just snug. Done.

Even though the clips have different colors on the metal 'spring' it looks like they'll all work. Also, I didn't realize it until i worked on it that the door has a latch on each side and ONLY ONE IS USED TO LATCH THE DOOR on the Duet Sport. i could have just used the other to replace the broken one.

Compare old element to provided picture. - Before you order your replacement element turn off the power (I turned off the 50 amp breaker in the breaker box) and remove old element so you can see the type of connections. Even though you have a correct cross over number for the element it might not be the same. Compare your element with the provided pictures making sure they look alike. In my case the connecting terminals were spay (slide on) and the element had a bend which matched the provided picture. It takes a ¼ nut driver to loosen to two machine screws from the mount. Needle nose or diagonal side cutters to remove the wires. Tip the front of the element up and pull back and the element comes out showing the connecting wires. Very carefully remove wires from each side and re attach to the new the element and reverse the take out step and re install. After mount screws are secure reset your power. Test and preheat the oven. It took less than a half an hour to complete the install. Excellent Value, Great Price. Shipping was on time.

The washer does require a monthly Affresh cleaning tablet. I would not miss this step because what I read is that odors build up in these HD machines. I also leave my lid open and the little detergent drawer open to air it and dry it out after each laundry day.

I only use liquid HD detergent; powder may not always dissolve. I also don't use much detergent, depending on the soil level. Made in China. It's nice as long as you have the right expectations. - I’ve used a couple of these icemakers. There are quite a few of them being sold by different Chinese companies on Amazon right now. They may look slightly different, but they all operate the same. As long as you have proper expectations, they work fairly well.

The listing shows that this icemaker can make 27 pounds of ice per day. That would only be the case if someone empties the ice basket each and every time that it is full. It takes about an hour for it to feel, so you would have to have someone to constantly empty it, which is probably not going to happen.

This icemaker makes 9 cubes of ice at a time. They then empty into the holding basket which is on top of the water reservoir. Once the basket is full, it will stop making ice. If you do not remove the ice than the eye simply melts back down into the water reservoir, and the process starts all over again. You can remove the ice cubes and place them in a freezer, but the ice cubes are wet so when you place the cubes into the freezer they will freeze together in a clump. So you have to use an ice pick or something else to break them apart.

It’s best to turn this icemaker off before you go to bed, or when you are leaving the office, and not let it run when no one is there to use or remove the ice. Otherwise, as stated above, the eye simply melts in the process of refreezing continues again and again.

This icemaker is made in China and being sold by Chinese company on Amazon.

And then I found an old guy showing that you don't have to remove the complete back panel since it's flexible and you can leave the ice maker in place! (Pull out the ice maker drawer, however.) He used a tie wrap (I used a piece of yarn - cause that's what I had nearby and I'm just an 'old' lady, lol) and after you take out the bottom most 5 screws you flex the panel up and tie it through the screw hole to the ice maker bracket to get it out of your way.

I turned off my circuit at the breaker box so I didn't even have to pull out the fridge from the wall to unplug it. Take ice make drawer out, remove the shelves and bottom basket, take 5 screws out and tie panel up to the ice maker bracket, remove motor, remove fan from old and put on new, put back in place, screw the back panel down, replace shelves and you're done. :) (Oh, and turn the breaker back on.)

Does not filter water in a measurable way. - Aqua-Pure filters are made in the US under license from the patent holder. This is a cheap Chinese knock-off of uncertain quality. Do not buy this POS if you want a real Aqua-Pure filter.

I tested it with the TDS meter I use to monitor the RO/DI water purifier I use for my saltwater aquarium. First, I ran 5 gallons of water through this filter installed in my Samsung fridge. The water was black for a while, but it cleared up by gallon 3. Instructions say run it for 5 minutes to flush carbon dust, and it took about 7 minutes to pull 5 G.

Measured TDS for the "Aqua-Pure compatible" was 138 PPM. Then I measured unfiltered tap water, and once again got 138 PPM. I repeated the test three times on each water source and got the same figures, +/- 1 PPM.

Consequently, I know that this device does not filter water at all and is certainly not compatible with Aqua Pure. It works no better than having no filter at all in the fridge.

UPDATE 2: The genuine Aqua Pure doesn't reduce TDS either, so it appears that fridge filters are a waste of money even when they're not falsely promoted.

Worked With Slight Modification - I needed this for a Kenmore double oven gas stove. The proper item (with screw tab that mounts the igniter on its edge) was $112 and up. This one worked fine with a minor modification. I had to carefully bend the screw tab downward in order to mount it on its edge. The other tab had to be cut off; which I did with a Dremel tool using a diamond cutoff wheel. Took all of about 5 minutes. I removed the plug from the old igniter and using the included ceramic wire nuts, attached the plug to the new igniter. Another reviewer stated his wire nut did not want to lock on to the wires and apparently fell off, shorting and knocking out his control board. I experienced similar but remedied the problem by nipping (shortening) the bare wires. He apparently had his wire a bit too long and it bottomed out in the wire nut before it could grip and lock on. After nipping off about 1/16th in. the nut tightened properly and securely. The oven now works just fine. Note* As others have stated, just because your igniter glows does not mean it is good....it may not be getting hot enough to activate the temperature sensor to turn on the gas.

The other thing I had to figure out is that when I do want to use a store-bought K-cup - which I sometimes do if they are on sale - then I need to put the old K-cup part back in (the one I removed and replaced with the universal one) so that the store-bought K-cup fits again. It's not hard to swap them out after you do it once.

I really hope this helps the other people who didn't think this fit their machine. I have the Classic K 55 machine, by the way.

Install tips - The pump is pretty straight forward to install. I suggest tipping the washer forward onto a pad for easy access to the pump and protection of the washer. The only difficult bit is installing the fuse. The directions are a little vague on this (and there are two options on where to install the fuse depending on the exact model of washer you have). The fuse is added into the console (the part on the top of the washer that has the key-pad on it). To get access to the area where you need to add the fuse, you need to 1) remove the lid of the washer (swing it straight up into the position it would be when you add clothes and then pull the lid straight up) and 2) remove two screws from the back of the console.
Then the scary bit - you will need to find the correct wire based on the directions (make sure you are following the correct directions for your model!) and then cut the wire and strip the ends. The fuse holder has a single red wire that you will need to cut in two (and strip the ends). Then twist the wires together and crimp with the included connectors. You will need a wire stripper and crimper in addition to a common Phillips head screwdriver. Not hard to do if you have done light home repair jobs before.

Very sturdy & well made hat washer - I have an existing hat washer from another brand. I wanted to get another one so that I could wash 2 caps at the same time. I saw this available via the Vine program. I placed the order and it was delivered within 2 days.

Here's my initial impressions of the new one (black) vs the old one (white)
- The new hat washer is much more robust & sturdy, quality is better than the old one
- The new hat washer comes in 3 parts; the old one with 2 pieces
- Even though it appears that you could wash 2 hats simultaneously with the new hat washer, it's recommended to wash only 1 at a time
- The multiple latch points of the new hat washer secures the hat better than the old one; this greatly reduces the risk of the hat washer unexpectedly opening up in the dishwasher
- The new hat washer is slightly longer than the old one (0.50 inch); this may or may not make a difference when placing it in the dishwasher
- The double-sided instructions that accompany the new hat washer are very clear & helpful; the insert for the old hat washer had a few lines that didn't really say much
- Both hat washers work very well in the dishwasher
- The new hat washer can be used in a washing machine on gentle cycle. I haven't tried it yet, but will do so soon; I would never even attempt to use the old hat washer in a washing machine

Overall, I think this new hat washer is great. It's definitely better than the one I already had. I have more flexibility when it comes to washing hats (washing machine vs dishwasher). And now I can wash 2 hats at the same time.

Recycle Hack - Well, anyone who owns a Samsung French Door Refrig with a POS Ice Room Ice Maker knows that even after applying all the fixes, they'll still be hair-dryer defrosting it, every ~3 months; I've got it down to ~15 minutes now. So instead of buying a new refrigerator-with-ice-maker-in-the-freezer-drawer (at C0stc0), I decided to limp it along another year and buy another filter. There's just the two of us in the household and I've calculated we dispense <300gal through the filter annually PLUS we have a clean water supply, so I ignore the 6 month reminder and replace it every December.
The filter is a simple plastic 1/4" thick, two piece plastic cartridge with 3 rubber o-rings, housing the carbon-filter insert. It's not difficult to disassemble the filter for recycling/disposal:
1) remove the o-rings with an awl or precision mini bladed screwdriver. shake out the water.
2) clamp the filter in a vise or brace appropriately
3) (hack)saw 1/4" deep around the diameter at the cartridge seam, about 1/3 up from the bottom.
4) discard the carbon-filter insert and recycle the two plastic cartridge pieces.
Maybe call your recycler and confirm they recycle Acrylonitrile Butadiene Styrene (ABS) (7).
Remember to run 3 gallons of water through your new filter. Maybe water the plants, fill a toilet tank, or clean the sinks and use it for rinse water.

Actionable bundle of technology - The primary purpose of this AcuRite Indoor Air Quality Monitor is an alert to turn on the humidifier for sensitive family members. It's dimmable and legible. The sampling rate and screen update are appropriate.

Depending on your use, this monitor measures @PM2.5. It's an appropriate indoor green/yellow/red light monitor. @PM2.5 ≤ 12µ = green light. Yellow light between 13-35. >35? Deepening shades of red ... until you can't see color, then like-2000 years in the future, some kid will be digging a hole and strike a void, someone will pour plaster of Paris in the void and you'll live in fame, slain by flaming hot particles just like Pompeii. @PM2.5 the results are comparable to the Air Quality Index (AQI) as locally reported by NOAA.

Relative humidity (RH%) is heuristically linked to PM2.5. The higher the RH%, the lower the PM2.5. The lower the RH%, the higher the PM2.5 reading. I’ve noticed that an interior RH% ≈ 50% displays 1-5 ppm.

As a note to ‘bunny suit’ people, PM2.5 is not the metric for comparisons to ISO cleanroom levels. This monitor might suggest 1-5 ppm, but, my living room is NOT class 10 ... given rugs, etc, it can't be made to get to class 100,000.

Twenty years ago, this sensor was a high-$ industrial proposition and hardly for home use. However, Acurite has packaged a bundle of technology here to deliver excellent value for money.

Affordable replacement for OEM fridge filters - I wanted to post a review on these filters to clear some things up. One of the leading negative reviews points out that the openings are different shapes from the original. This is true, but if the reviewer had taken a moment to look into their filter housing they would realize that this hole shape does not matter. This is simply an opening for water to flow. Water doesn't care if it is a square or round hole it is passing through. If you look at the housing you will see that the filter seals to the housing where the two O-rings are. The inner hole could be a triangle for all it matters. The inner hole has no way of creating a leak.

With that said. The filter has worked well for the past month of so that I have had it installed. A cheap alternative to OEM filters. We've all seen how cheap brand name filters can be from refillable pitchers. This is essentially the same thing but sealed, there is no reason a "cheap" filter should be too hard to believe.

I had to press out the bearings from the broken wheel only to realize they were slightly bigger than the original wheel bushing. Finally, I pressed the new bearings into the old wheel, and installed the old wheel onto the new arm. The good news. Make sure to troubleshoot and replace all parts while you have the dryer opened up - My 20 year old dryer decided that it was going to heat at it's hottest setting to the point of scalding my hands when removing the clothes from the dryer and causing a major case of wrinkles in my work Polo's. After going to YouTube to find out how to diagnose the issue, I found that there are a few things to check. First thing you will need to do is open the back of the dryer, with it unplugged, and check the Thermal Fuse. This can be done with a multi-meter or temporarily jump the two connectors/blade terminals and check if the Dryer runs at the correct temp for all cycles. Since I had the dryer taken apart I figured I would clean out the blower fan area and the fan ducting as well as the entire "innards" of the dryer. After temporarily jumping the thermal fuse I found that it had kicked the bucket as the dryer started to work again due to jumping out the fuse. Did I say that this dryer is 20 years old and the original fuse lasted that long? So I decided that since I have the thing open I might as well replace the other 20 Year old electrical components that were back there. These Items included: the Thermal Fuse, Cycling Thermostat, High Limit Dryer Thermostat and Dryer Thermal cut off. One thing I've learned with these stainless steel filters is that you cannot use finely ground coffee in them or they get gunked up and no longer work. The key, apparently, is to clean them immediately after use, but what does that mean?

This Nuben filter came with clear instructions on how to clean the filter (I will use a bamboo toothbrush) and what to do if it does get gunked up (you essentially burn the accumulated debris to ash in a very hot oven, then brush it out!). As with any pour-over (except for Oxo's, which takes care of it for you), you pour a little, wait about 30 seconds for the grounds to bloom, then finish the pour by spiraling out from the center. But because the water is dripping through fairly quickly, how do you know when you've poured too much?

I'll figure it out.

Simple replacement, inexpensive, metal - DON'T REMOVE THE RIVETS!!
I have a Kenmore Elite hood and wasn't sure if these would work, but since the photos of the hood appeared very similar to mine, I figured I'd try them since both sides of the center one was broken 11 years ago when I moved in, and now another side broke. I'm not a duct tape person and my screens need to be in place.

My old brackets are plastic (these are spring metal with a hole in the center!) so I carefully bent and broke off the remaining bracket and a half. I left the 3 rivets intact, cleaned the areas with alcohol where the new ones would adhere, dried them and cleaned and dried them again. You can make it work - The description says it can be expanded to 29.5 inches (75cm) but if you do that, the aluminum bars holding it to the corners will have less than 1 inch of the bar inside of each end. This is not enough to hold 440 lbs. I would say that 30 lbs at full extension is about all it will hold up. The only way it will hold 440 lbs is when the unit is fully collapsed and that size was too small for my refrigerator. The aluminum bars are 1-inch square bars that slide into the corner piece made of heavy-duty plastic and that snug connection gives the stand its strength. The aluminum bars are very very thin and upgrading the quality of the bars will give a lot of strength to the stand. As-is, this unit would not hold the Galanz refrigerator I have pictured.

I did modify the stand. First I threw away the cheap aluminum bars. I could bend them with my bare hands without much difficulty. Next, I went to a big box home improvement store and purchased a 1-inch square steel bar (which cost more than the stand). After cutting the steel bar to length and tapping them into the corner pieces, the strength became a lot more than 440 lbs.

Bottom line is that as described, the sturdiness of the stand reduces significantly as you expand the stand length and width. The specs must describe the stand when it's fully collapsed. With a little know-how, you can make this work better by upgrading the length and strength of the bars.

Works.....now - This unit is OK I guess for the money. The 1st time I used it, it made ice & filled the bin & shut down & never came back on. I tried a couple of things from the rather sparse troubleshooting guide to no avail. As a last ditch effort I plugged it back in one morning & at work, applied to return it. When I got home that evening, the bin was full of ice and it's worked fine ever since.
Apparently the mere threat of returning it to China was enough to get it to do what it was supposed to.
It is VERY noisey and mine appears to have a rattle somewhere near the fan. If I rap the side of it near the fan it stops for a few moments but then starts again.
The ice it produces is very porous and melts very quickly in a drink...which is OK since I just use it for water but in mixed drinks and soda, etc, it would water it down very quickly. You can put some of the ice into baggies & put in your freezer to harden but that's why I bought this unit...I didn't want to take up space in my small apartment-sized fridge to make and store ice.
The way the system is designed, the unit doesn't hold the ice below freezing so after dumping into the bin, it begins to melt. The water from melting goes back into the water supply tank and is used again to make ice over and over. I strongly recommend using filtered water like a Brita pitcher to fill the tank. The ice produced will not have a taste to it like using tap water. The water in the tank will also last longer. The instructions recommend draining the water from the tank every day. That would be a total pain and using filtered water I just do it about once a week or every few days if I'm not using a lot of ice.
Bottom line, if you're wanting an ice maker to use behind your home wet bar, keep looking and spend the money for a higher quality unit. If you just want some ice in your water, this unit is OK for that.

The new design has a wire basket with a lid, like the old one, but the basket then goes inside a plastic shell with a single hole in the bottom. So preparing one for use requires two steps instead of one, and cleaning is a pain. The old basket had a "handle" that I used to rap on the edge of a bowl to shake the grounds loose (I save my grounds for gardening). Also, the new design allows you to make either a cup or a carafe. Okay, not a bad idea, except that now you have to go through another menu, in which you must select either a picture of a carafe or a number, 1-6; then you get to another screen where you can select the size. There's really no explanation of what the numbers mean (I know, it's probably in the Keurig manual somewhere) so we just guess and then see what we get.
The whole thing is annoying. Amazon is famous for reducing transactional friction; it's disappointing when a company goes out of its way to increase friction.
On the plus side, a cup of coffee seems to brew more quickly. Haven't actually timed the two models, but it feels faster.
Regarding Keurig customer service: I recently posted a question about the cracking lids, and someone from Keurig suggested that I call customer support. I did, and it was a waste of time. Does not reduce Total Dissolved Solids (TDS) - You may find reviews discounting the importance of a TDS measurement talking about what it doesn't measure. Those miss the point. Ok, there might be some other bad stuff that might get removed that is not part of a TDS measurement. That's great. However, that doesn't change the fact that TDS is measuring OTHER CONTAMINANTS THAT STILL REMAIN.

The Environmental Protection Agency's (EPA's) National Secondary Drinking Water Regulations (NSDWRs) limit TDS to 500mg/L. This filter does not reduce TDS below this level.

From the Environmental Protection Agency's Website:

National Secondary Drinking Water Regulations (NSDWRs)
NSDWRs (or secondary standards) are non-enforceable guidelines regulating contaminants that may cause cosmetic effects (such as skin or tooth discoloration) or aesthetic effects (such as taste, odor, or color) in drinking water. EPA recommends secondary standards to water systems but does not require systems to comply with the standard. However, states may choose to adopt them as enforceable standards

This may or may not filter metals and other contaminants--read the fine print - ANSI/NSF 42 compliance does not perform to the same level as ANSI/NSF 53. So while I went through three of these and am now looking to re-order, I discovered that other types can be both 42 and 53 compliant, meaning they also filters heavy metals, whereas these Water Sentinels are not certified to do so. However, as you will see in one of the replies to this, the manufacturer claims it is built to the 53 standard but is in an extended process of certification.

So while the LG part costs more, you are getting a product that has been certified to perform better. I will opt for the LG for now, since one can never know what metals, benzene, and other contaminants may be in your local water supply, but you may make your own decision as to whether the manufacturer can be taken at their word. You can search google for the difference in standards, but here is a link: http://www.wqpmag.com/not-all-filters-are-created-or-tested-equal, where it explains 42 aims for taste and odor ONLY, and 53 aims for health-related claims.

As for how these actually make the water taste, I had no issues at all with that, and they worked properly for six months each, so for that reason along I might recommend them to those on a tight budget. I would guess that people with softer water can expect more longevity from these than those with hard water.

Chances are the vent's wiring is copper. However, this product's wiring is aluminum. DO NOT simply solder or connect aluminum to copper. They have different heating temperatures and if your fan is in a bathroom, moisture will corrode the wiring.

I'm not an electrician fyi. But after some research, you need to buy copper to aluminum connections. There's only a couple proprietary brands that are reliable but a quick search will show you the purple connection cones that work. (Thanks for the info Eric).
Oh, and one more thing, I had to reverse the engine rotation, it's easy, remove the nuts and bolts holding the shaft's bearings in position and reverse it once it has been removed, your fan should be spinning clockwise looking at it from behind the motor. As long as you use this properly it should work with the machine. If you don't it will poke a hole in it. The coffee works out well if you use it right.

There are a few important things to keep in mind

#1. This ice maker does NOT keep the ice which is made frozen. It drops into the bin. .. then melts and is recycled if you do not use it. If you want to keep it frozen. . . You'll need to place it into your own freezer.

#2. Though the listing shows that this ice maker can make 26# of ice in 24-hours. . . That's only if you have someone standing there to empty the bin each time it is full. . . day-and-night. So that part is really no realistic.

#3. "Self-Cleaning" is a misnomer. When you turn-on the "self-cleaning" cycle. .. All that happens is that the water is cycled through again and again until you stop it. So there's really not a lot of cleaning going on unless you add something to the water. There's no information about what to add. You can do your own research. . but. . . I actually use the same cleaner I use with my espresso maker for descaling.

Stops a Speed Queen washer from walking around the laundry room - We have a Speed Queen Commercial washing machine ( LFNE5BSP113TW01) in our home. This thing is a 270 pound beast, and it really cleans so much better than the newer Samsung it replaced. The issue that I had with it is that it is installed on a tile floor that is a little slippery. This washer uses more water than most front loaders (probably the reason it actually gets clothes clean), and when it enters the rinse or spin cycles, it will naturally oscillate a little while it balances the load. When the washer would oscillate, it would slowly walk around to a spot where it was no longer in balance on the floor (it's a tile floor, and not perfectly level in all spots). When it hit that place, it would start vibrating and dancing around like crazy. If you gave it a gentle push back to it's original position, the vibration would cease immediately. I needed some pads to keep this machine from moving on the floor, and absorb some of the vibration, and these have done the job perfectly. The washer is so much quieter now, and I'm sure that is resulting in less wear on the machine. I was concerned whether or not these would be large enough inside diameter for this big washer, but they fit perfectly, and they work great!. Front load washers ought to be shipped with these things.

Consider getting a transparent hose - Is this a dishwasher hose or a clothes-washing machine hose? It seems targeted at both since it has the bracket for a washing machine and the universal end for a dishwasher. Both hose types are essentially the same as long as they fit. This product is more suitable for a washing machine than a dishwasher, but it should work for both.

This is a fine dishwasher hose that you can cut to the right exit diameter. In addition to the exit diameter, make sure the end will fit as there are L-shaped and straight ends. For going into the garbage disposal, having a straight end at that location reduces clogging. Confirm the length you need. If you need to wrap the hose over the top of the dishwasher to get to the drain then 6 ft will not be long enough. This comes with two smaller clamps and one larger clamp, in addition to the extension connector and a hose holder if this is used with a clothes washing machine. For a washing machine, 6ft should be fine.

I have done a lot of dishwasher troubleshooting as a manager of rental properties. Most dishwasher drain hoses I encounter are somewhat transparent. I can see water and debris flowing through them and can see accumulated debris. This is useful when troubleshooting a drainage issue or investigating a possible clog. While not essential, since transparent hoses are so readily available, why not get one of those instead of this opaque one? The transparent ones are the hazy white-colored one that allows light through. I have never had a washing machine drain clog, so for that this opaque color is fine.

This is a generic Chinese hose and the identical product is being sold under different Amazon listings.

1. Uses a standard Edison plug (i.e. parallel blade with a ground). This can be either a pro or a con. For me it was problematic because the outlet for my washer and dryer was on only a 20 amp circuit. A 30-amp dryer plug would have been more convenient for me. That said, it is nice to know that I can use this dryer if my next apartment doesn't have a dryer outlet.
2. Decent little workhorse--takes some time to get things dry, but it does what it's designed to do.
3. Lightweight--I don't feel like I'll be over-burdening my friends if I ever ask them to help me move.
Cons:
1. It's far too short -- plan on either mounting it to the wall, building a pedestal, or developing back problems. If I were to recommend a redesign for the next model it would be to put the controls near the top.
2. The vent on the back is a non-standard size (about 3 3/8 inches). This made putting a dryer tube on the back a pain. I followed the advice of another reviewer and removed some of the wire from a 4" wide flexible aluminum duct and was able to clamp it on with some careful finagling.
3. Drum wouldn't spin on first running the machine. I had to open it up and wrap the belt around the drum to get it to spin (I don't really knock stars off for this, since it happens from time to time; but I mention it for anyone who does buy it--if it doesn't spin at first, unplug it, take of the back panel and have a look before returning it -- saved me a shipping headache).

Overall:
If your choice is no dryer or this dryer, buy this dryer. I really like having a dryer, but I don't particularly like having this dryer. Between it's height and the difficulty attaching the hose to the vent, I don't think I'd buy it again. That said, it is a decent bargain, and it does the job I need it to do. I can't hate it too much.

Defeats the purpose of a Keurig - A Keurig will give you a great cup of coffee, but you don't need a Keurig for that. What makes a Keurig unique is that it brews a cup of coffee faster and easier than any other method -- no carafe to clean, no filters to purchase, and no need to grind beans or measure ground coffee. Just pop in a K-cup and presto! In about two minutes you have coffee. Cleanup is restricted to your cup (and throwing away the used K-cup).

Using a "My K-cup" filter assembly with your own coffee really defeats the purpose of having a Keurig. You have to remove the original assembly (don't lose it!), measure your own coffee (which takes adjustment; you'll probably go through several cups of coffee before you get the measurement to your satisfaction), and clean everything up afterward (it can make a bit of a mess). This is really about as much trouble as just using a conventional little drip coffeemaker. In fact, to me it is MORE trouble, although I think the Keurig uses a bit less coffee and could save some money.

So there you have it. Using a Keurig in the conventional way is the most convenient but also the most expensive way to brew coffee, but using a My K-cup filter saves money at the expense of the convenience.

Poorly Designed - Save your money. The concept is appealing - "get those pesky coffee grounds into those reusable K-cups without making a huge mess." The sad part is, this COULD have been an awesome product if it were designed properly. Even worse, I have the mechanical aptitude of an eggplant, and even I can see the design flaw. Here's the concept: stick this device into the bag of coffee grounds, grab a scoopful with the closed end, and close the funnel end on top of it. Then stick your K-cup on top of the funnel, turn the device and K-cup upside down, and the grounds go neatly into the K-cup. Not rocket science, right? Unfortunately, the stem has a "male" ridge on the funnel side, and a "female" groove on the closed scoop side to keep the scoop and funnel aligned. What happens is the coffee grounds get into the groove when you scoop up the coffee grounds, and when you turn the device upside down to put the grounds into your K-cup, the grounds in the groove get released all over your work surface. So you've spent about $10, and you STILL have a mess. Had the groove been on the funnel side and the ridge on the scoop side, it would work fine. For me, a set of oblong measuring spoons from the dollar store does the job far more effectively and neatly. What to do with this? Maybe I can use it to harvest the doggie-doo from my chihuahua off my lawn. It sure doesn't work for transferring coffee grounds from the bag to the K-cup.

Seems to work, simple to use - We've had our pedestal humidifier for 3 weeks, and have been very pleased with it so far. I've added the bacteriostatic solution 2-3 times a week, and so far haven't noticed any musty smells.

We live in northern Colorado, and it's very dry, and we've been running the humidifier continuously since we got it. I haven't noticed any adverse effects on the wick from using the bacteriostatic solution. Prior to first using the bacteriostatic solution, the wick developed a brownish area on the topmost air intake side of the wick, about 1/5 of the wick size. The wick remained wet there. After a week or so, I rotated the wick so that the brown portion was in the water bath, and the brown color went away. The new topmost air intake side turned brown just like before, but was still wet. Using the bacteriostatic solution hasn't had any impact on the brown area, or how wet the wick gets.

The solution has chemical product warnings on it, and says to add "1/8 of a capful to a gallon of water." The active ingredient to the solution is an ammonia compound, so safety warnings are appropriate. Measuring 1/8 of a capful is an approximate measurement, and that doesn't present much of a challenge if you add about that much to the cap once, see about how much that is, and thereafter add that amount directly to the water you're adding.

A few tips from my installation experience:

(1) Make sure yor drill a hole in your over-the-range cabinet about 1mm wider than 6 inches
(2) Make sure the 6 inch hole is located at the same distance from the back wall. The product does not come up with a paper template. It makes drilling the correct holes near impossible.
(3) This thing is HEAVY at around 35lb. You will need 2 people to do it right.
(4) The screws that come with the product are too short. I ended up using my own.
(5) The grills are very tight to be removed. Each grill fin is super sharp. Watch your fingers (I got 2 cuts)

The thing I hate:
(a) The cable length is a total joke ... why only 3 inches out (if from the top) or 1 inch out (if from the rear) if it does not come with a power plug? So, when you install, you need to be very precise in drilling a 2-3 inches hole in the cabinet that match the power wires.

I did it all by myself in an hour. The exhaust/suction power is very good. My cabinet is about 3 ft from the range. I think the optimal distance is about 2ft. So this is something to be mindful if you have a low oven range.

Check your air vent gasket before ordering - Used this replacement gasket on a Kenmore 665.13402N411 dishwasher (2015). This is correct gasket to replace original on air vent W10469575. OEM gasket on vent was glued in. All videos I saw showed easy removal of old and fit of new. More of a project than I was expecting. I heated the gasket with a hair dryer and started pulling it out about 1/2" at a time. For more stubborn areas I dripped mineral spirits on the remaining gasket bits and let them sit for about 15-20 minutes then used an Xacto knife and a small plastic tool to remove the rest. Cleaned with soap and water dried 100% THEN fitted the new gasket. It stopped leaking by 99% and I think it is getting seated. However...

Check your leaking gasket to make sure it has easy removal. If not order part W10469575 if fan inside the door is still working. W10469574 if fan is kaput. Sears Parts Direct has the best videos I have found.

Gasket seems to be ok. Time will tell if it gets seated 100%. Shame on Whirlpool for using a rubber type glue to seat the OEM gasket.

UPDATE: we've run about (5) loads of dishes, pans, etc. through the dishwasher and the leak seems to have stopped completely. Rating now at (5) stars.

It has happened several times to both my partner & myself without noticing until we smell gas. Happens when we're cooking, sometimes happens we reach up to use the microwave above the stove, happened when our dog tried to stove surf-which really freaked us out.
Just yesterday a friend was over and began fixing a cup of coffee on the counter, next to the stove. I guess she may have grazed it with her body as she moved, within a few minutes we all began to smell gas, and we knew just where to check. Sure enough, the damn knob(s).
Some of the knobs seem to protrude out slightly further than the bar/oven handle-so the handle offers no protection of the knobs getting bumped.
Not sure if this problem is limited to our stove, but I would seriously check this stove out in person at a store first before purchasing.

I am not sure where/who to report this potentially deadly problem to, but thought I mention it here first where there is a significant amt of traffic.

Cheaper sets don't work as well - I tried to save a few bucks by buying a cheaper set of these suspension rods. They worked okay for a short while but just couldn't stabilize large loads in the washer. The slamming resumed.

I watched a few online videos and found (according to a couple of videos I found online, so take it with a grain of salt) that it's not the springs that are the key to how these rods work. It's the cap on top of the spring. The cap has a collar that fits rather tightly on the rod and slides up and down, but with some resistance. Apparently that resistance is what provides the damping and stops the slamming. When that collar loosens over time and the cap slides too easily, the slamming starts.

I saw some innovative fixes. One was to use construction adhesive around the collar to increase the friction. Another was to put a small cable tie around the collar and cinch it tightly enough to increase it.

Or you could just buy this set of replacement rods. This set works. Washer is slamming no more. Several videos are available online that show how to install them.

They've been going on 2 years now without changing the filter just because they never thought of a need to do so. Our family had been noticing that the water pressure for the in-door dispenser had been slowed to a slow trickle and that the ice was starting to have grains of who knows what in the cubes. I asked if they had changed the filter, and they were unaware that there was a filter to even change. Install was very simple. The filter was located in the upper right corner of the main compartment. To remove the filter, all I had to do was push in until I felt a click and pull the old filter out. I've use older style filters before with instructions to soak the filter for 30 minutes prior to install, but this one did not mention it. I removed the two plastic covers from the nipple end, lined up the plastic fins, and pushed the new filter in until I felt/heard a click. That was it......installed...... Next I ran the in door water for about 3 minutes or so to get all the air out the line and completely fill the filter as per the directions. I also tossed out the old ice so everyone could enjoy some fresh, clean ice. After about 10 minutes of work, we can all now enjoy better water pressure at the door with clean taste and clean ice. Great value for the price. Word of advise: I know manufacturers recommend replacing every 6 months, but save yourself some money and wait for an actual change in performance: pressure drop, change in flavor, or impurities in ice. UPDATE 25 Feb 2017: as noted by other reviewers, even if you rinse this immediately after each use, this filter can become clogged after a bit. HOWEVER, IT IS NOT HARD TO CLEAN! Put 3-4 cups of water to boil in a pot on the stove (or fill the pot with hot water from your kettle to speed up the process). With the burner still on medium to medium-high, add 1 cup of plain white vinegar. Lower the coffee filter into the pot so that the drip end is at the bottom of the pot. Let it boil for a few minutes. Using the silicone tab, lift the filter out of the pot to see if the water is draining through freely. If not, continue to boil the filter until the water drains freely when you lift the filter out of the pot. Once it does drain freely, take the filter out of the pot, set it in the cup stand, and set the filter and stand in the sink. Pour the boiling vinegar water through the filter and let it drain out into the sink. Let the filter dry completely before the next use so that the vinegar completely evaporates. The filter is as good as new after this, and we don't taste any vinegar, either. But if you want to be extra sure, you can add a plain hot water rinse at the end of the process to wash away all the vinegar. ALL filters will clog after awhile, and cleaning them is a normal part of ownership.

A little messy, but works great! - My washing machine broke at the start of the recent quarantine, and I'm still waiting for an appointment to have it fixed. With most laundromats closed, in desperation I bought a Wonderwash, hoping it would tide me over until I can get my washing machine fixed.

This little machine is great! It is well-made and all the parts feel sturdy and high-quality. It arrives unassembled but is a breeze to put together, it takes five minutes and no tools. I highly recommend watching one of the instructional Youtube videos before doing your first load of wash, it explains the process thoroughly, but the basics are: determine load size, add a small amount of detergent and fill with hot or warm water to the fill line. Add clothes, tighten down the lid, then just turn the crank for two minutes or so (I time it by listening to a song on the radio.)

The key is to turn the crank slowly, not quickly, and let the wet laundry fall from the top of the chamber to the bottom with a good thud each time. This drives the water and soap through the clothes and cleans them thoroughly. Once you're done, drain the chamber using the supplied pipe, then refill with cool water to the fill line and crank for two minutes again to rinse.

My clothes came out really clean! Even garments with cooking stains washed right up. The only drawbacks are that water tends to splatter around a bit when you drain the chamber, and I found that to drain it completely when I was done I needed to turn the whole chamber upside down and let it set for a bit. I use the Wonderwash in my bathtub, so a little bit of water splashing around is not an issue.

Other than that, this is a perfect little machine for doing small loads of laundry. It was a desperation buy, but I am really pleased with it! After my main washer is fixed, I intend to keep it to use in my RV camper. It would also be great for dorm or apartment dwellers.

If you don't do that then eventually nothing will come out except the noise of the ice maker. This is actually not a big deal however. I would still buy this refrigerator even with the incompetently designed ice maker. It does make one wonder, though. Something like this isn't designed by idiots. Why make a chute shaped like a rectangle with corners for ice to accumulate in?

So overall, a great refrigerator with a non-fatal flaw.

Make sure you know how this machine works before purchasing. - If you have a look around Amazon, you will see that there are lots… And lots… And lots of these icemakers listed by Chinese companies on Amazon right now. Some of them look a little different from each other, but they all basically work the same. As long as you have the right expectations, they work very well. But if your expectations are too high, you will be very disappointed.

Some of the basic things you need to know about this icemaker… First of all, it is not connected to a water source. You pour water into the reservoir. Next, the ice is not kept frozen inside. The machine will make ice until the bin is full. Then the ice will melt, if not removed from the bin, and will be recycled again and again and again. Freezing… Melting… Freezing… Melting… And so on. For this reason, you really need to turn it off at night when you’re sleeping or when you leave the office, if you are using it in an office environment.

When the bin is full, which takes about an hour, you will have enough ice to fill a 32 ounce water bottle. Though the listing shows that it will make 26 pounds of ice within twenty-four hours, that is only possible if someone is going to remove the ice each time the bin is full… Day and night. If you want to make ice and save it, then you will need to place it into your own freezer. But keep in mind that the ice will be “wet” so when you place it into your own freezer it will freeze together and you will need to break it apart to use it.

This icemaker is made in China and being sold by Chinese company on Amazon.

They also included three little metal push-on connectors which in some cases you need to attach to the wires. You cut off the old connector, strip off a bit of insulation, twist and insert the wire into the new connector, and crimp it to stay on. Easy.

The new connectors they sent were designed for a 1/8-inch wide metal prong on the new motor. I ran into one problem because on my dryer, the yellow wire was actually two wires inserted together into the old connector, and it did not appear the new connector could handle two wires going in. But I had an extra connector from what they sent me, and the spot where the yellow attaches had two prongs (coming from the same piece of metal), so I attached one connector to each yellow wire separately. However, one prong was just a bit wider than 1/8 inch, so the new connector would not push on. I went to Home Depot and the narrowest connector they had was 1/4 inch, but it could take two wires, so I used one of those. Hopefully it will be okay that a 1/4-inch connector is pushed onto a metal prong that is a bit narrower than that. It seemed like a tight enough fit.

Must have for igniter issues on a Whirlpool SF362LXSQ 30" Accubake! - I purchased this item about one year ago to fix my Whirlpool oven model SF362LXSQ 30" Accubake which was not igniting or heating up. I also purchased two other components because I didn't want to waste my time taking the oven apart to find out it was something else so I purchased these two additional parts all from Amazon: Whirlpool W10293048 Gas Valve for Range and Whirlpool 8054129 Oven Igniter for Range. I replaced all three parts in my Whirlpool model and so far, one year later, the oven is working perfectly. I had the Whirlpool oven for about 4 years before the broiler died (1st thing to die) and I ignored it because I could live without the feature. Then three years later the oven won't ignite so I couldn't bake (2nd thing to die). This time, I had to do something because unlike broiling, I actually need to be able to bake to make pizzas in the oven. I researched online about what could be the cause and read about solenoid and amperage issues. I checked each solenoid for 216 Ohms resistance (Broil to Common and Bake to Common). I did find that one of the solenoid was defective. If any one is defective neither will operate and the gas valve/regulator has to be replaced. Beware: Check the NSF ratings - This product is supposedly certified to the NSF 42 & 372 standards. However, NSF 42 means it "reduces aesthetic impurities such as chlorine and taste/odor ". And NSF 372 means the product does not leach lead into the water (i.e. it says nothing about whether or not it removes lead from the water).

The important NSF standards for water filtration are NSF 42, 53, 401. NSF 53 is designed to "reduce specific health-related contaminants." NSF 401 is designed to "remove up to 15 individual contaminants which
have been identified in published studies as occurring in drinking water."

So if you only care about NSF 42 (taste) and care less about actual health-related contaminants, these filters seem fine. If you care about health-related contaminants, I'd look elsewhere.

Replaced Whirlpool (wdt710paym6) Dishwasher element , but adjustments were needed. Includes nuts! - Listed as replacement part for W10518394 (Whirlpool part number for my dishwasher). I ultimately got it to work with my dishwasher, however, there are a few issues. It was the right shape and the element was the right size. The spade connectors were also the right fit for the electrical connections. But, 1. The threads do not match the original plastic nuts, so you cant use the original / more convenient nuts. I expected this, based reviews of many other elements being sold as replacements. Which is why I chose this particular one on Amazon because this seller was one of very few sellers that listed the item with included nuts. (Much appreciated! added the fourth star.) The ones that were included with this item worked fine, but a deep well socket is required / recommended to install them. I would also recommend installing them with a washer so that the edges of the nuts are not digging into the plastic dishwasher basin. 2. A little more of an issue, the threaded parts of the element were too wide to fit through the holes of the dishwasher basin. I may have been able to force it through but it would have required a significant amount of force and I did not want to risk damaging the dishwasher or the part. Instead, I used a Dremel to slightly widen the holes in the dishwasher basin (Very carefully, as I had to make sure the hole was small enough and uniform for the sealing washer to still seal). After making the above modifications, I was able to install the element. It is working well so far. No leaks. My dishwasher is drying once again and washing better as the water is actually hot throughout the cycle. I can recommend this item, just be prepared for some possible modifications.

This is a combination of a cap that has a pressure sensitive silicone release valve set into the middle of a solid bottom and a metal fine screen. You screw it onto the Aeropress instead of the usual cover.

THE BOTTOM LINE
A PERFECT addition to my Aeropress, this little beauty makes great coffee even better. It keeps the grounds in the water just long enough to make a truly good cup of coffee. I love how it works, and even don't mind losing the satisfaction of popping little pucks of coffee into the compost.

For example, this icemaker cannot keep the ice frozen. So the ice cubes are made… Placed into a basket… And then you either remove them and use them or place them into your own freezer. Otherwise the ice simply melts and then will be refrozen.

The listing shows that this icemaker can make up to 33 pounds of ice per day. That is a bit of a misnomer, because the only way it can do that is if you constantly remove the ice day and night. So if this icemaker is in a location where there are people there around-the-clock, then yes it can make up to 33 pounds per day. As long as the ice is constantly being removed. But if you are at home, and using it simply for your family, then of course while you are sleeping you are not going to be removing the ice. One very nice thing that this particular model has that many others do not is the option to use a timer so that it will start and stop when you wanted to and not continue to make ice when you don’t need it to, like when you are sleeping.

Tools required are a Phillips screw driver, a 17mm wrench or 17mm socket wrench, and lock-tight for assembly, you can get locktight at a hardware store or automotive parts store

Unplug power cord
Remove the 4 screws on the back panel
Remove the 17mm bolt on the rotor, you may need someone to hold the drum from spinning it will be a little hard to remove (lefty lucy, righty tighty)
slide the rotor off
Check stator for damage (if the motor ran the stator should be fine, also easy to replace)
Line up the splines on the shaft with the splines on the rotor and slide the new rotor on
reinstall bolt with locktight
reinstall panel
Done!

I’ve had it for several months, and it is consistently great and problem-free. It’s not super-easy to clean, but none of them are, and it is much easier than most. If you use purified water, the cubes will be perfect and crystal clear. I wish I only ever had used purified water, as it probably would have saved me some cleaning and descaling, but this was much easier than in other machines I’ve had. I read some reviews complaining that the ice doesn’t break automatically—I actually appreciate this very much because that also means it holds longer. You just take the ice sheets from the bottom of the stack, and then they’re easier to break, too. The machine also keeps it fairly cold, and it makes a boatload of ice in a day. Batches aren’t as “instant” as the bullet-style, but it doesn’t take that much longer, lasts much better in a drink, and if you just keep it filled and let it run, there’s always some ready. I’ve been doing this since I got it—I let it run all day and night. I leave it in the strainer without transferring to the freezer and use lots of ice throughout the day. If I ever have to buy another, I’ll buy this brand, but it’s been very reliable and consistent, so I’m not even sure I’ll have to get another. I suppose if you could shell out $400-500 for a luxury kind, you might be able to find a better one, but I’m exceedingly happy with this one, especially for the price. It’s very well-designed and well-constructed.

Research, Diagnose, change out all items that may fail.. - My 20 year old dryer decided that it was going to heat at it's hottest setting to the point of scalding my hands when removing the clothes from the dryer and causing a major case of wrinkles in my work Polo's. After going to YouTube to find out how to diagnose the issue, I found that there are a few things to check. First thing you will need to do is open the back of the dryer, with it unplugged, and check the Thermal Fuse. This can be done with a multi-meter or temporarily jump the two connectors/blade terminals and check if the Dryer runs at the correct temp for all cycles. Since I had the dryer taken apart I figured I would clean out the blower fan area and the fan ducting as well as the entire "innards" of the dryer. After temporarily jumping the thermal fuse I found that it had kicked the bucket as the dryer started to work again due to jumping out the fuse. Did I say that this dryer is 20 years old and the original fuse lasted that long? So I decided that since I have the thing open I might as well replace the other 20 Year old electrical components that were back there. These Items included: the Thermal Fuse, Cycling Thermostat, High Limit Dryer Thermostat and Dryer Thermal cut off. Each have their own job and purpose, so don't skimp out and think you can get away with changing the item that has failed, because if that item failed the others will follow. Did I mention my Dryer is 20 years old? As A side note; I also checked the Heating Element and found that one of the coils had warped and contacted/welded itself the the element body, this is what took out the fuse. A pair of needle nose pliers and a steady hand detached the coil and re-positioned the coil in its original shape and placement. My 20 year old dryer, that was a wedding gift to my wife when she married her fist husband now works like a champ!

After some tweaking, fantastic coffee! - Obviously, reviews on this are generally positive, but I'm the guy who checks out a product like this by searching "Ekobrew sucks", so I read through the negative reviews first. I ended up getting two of these anyway based on the rest of the reviews, and now that I've used them for a while, I'm really surprised at some of the negative responses and the difficulties they've had. The gasket on the lid is excellent, and I've not once had a leaking or overflow problem. Usually I would think that would be an issue of using grounds that are too fine and water not getting through. However, I use a Cuisinart burr grinder and grind on the next-to-finest grind, and fill it to the line and tap it down (tap, like on the table, not tamp, like with my fingers), and get a beautiful dark stream of coffee coming out, and I've never had it overflow once, so I wonder if others have been packing their coffee tight. Now, it does take longer for all the water to get through than it does for a regular k-cup, but that's a negligible issue. Best bet is to use a variable grinder like that and experiment a little with the grind size until your coffee comes out how you like it. I've found a medium/drip grind gives you five scoop Maxwell House, fine grind gives you French press. Yes, I do find more coffee solids on the bottom of my cup afterward, and I guess if you don't like that you'll have issues with this. If you are an espresso or French press lover, though, you're getting exactly what you like - dark coffee, nice brown crema, and yes, just a bit of coffee solids at the finish.

For clean up, do rinse these right away. If you let them sit and dry, it does take a little extra effort, but if you pull it out and rinse it right away, it cleans out quickly.

All in all, well worth both the savings, AND you get to use the coffee that you've always liked.
